---
# ============================================================================
# MY499 dissertation | Candidate 62628
# Renders to PDF. R chunks pull real tables/figures from output/.
# ============================================================================
format:
  pdf:
    pdf-engine: xelatex
    documentclass: scrartcl
    papersize: a4
    geometry: [margin=1in]
    number-sections: true
    toc: false
    colorlinks: true
    fig-pos: 'H'
    keep-tex: false
    cite-method: citeproc
    fontsize: 12pt
    linestretch: 2
    # Body, tables and figures are one typographic system: this font must match
    # THESIS_FONT in scripts/90_style.R. Change both together or not at all.
    # The OTFs ship with TinyTeX (tex-gyre, tex-gyre-math) and are copied to
    # ~/Library/Fonts so that ragg renders the figures in the same family.
    mainfont: "TeX Gyre Termes"
    mathfont: "TeX Gyre Termes Math"
    include-in-header:
      text: |
        % KOMA sets every heading, and every TOC entry, from `disposition`,
        % which defaults to sans-serif. Overriding it is what keeps the contents
        % page in the same family as the body.
        \setkomafont{disposition}{\normalfont\bfseries}
        % Section titles a touch larger; subheadings at body size. All bold,
        % sentence case, no small caps.
        \setkomafont{section}{\normalfont\large\bfseries}
        \setkomafont{subsection}{\normalfont\normalsize\bfseries}
        \setkomafont{subsubsection}{\normalfont\normalsize\bfseries\itshape}
        % Quarto wraps a captioned table in its own float, so kableExtra's
        % HOLD_position applies to the inner tabular and the outer float still
        % drifts -- which put the framework table above the section heading that
        % introduces it. Pinning the default placement fixes every table at once.
        \usepackage{float}
        \floatplacement{table}{H}
        % [H] takes the table out of the float mechanism and places it in the
        % text flow, where it inherits the document's double spacing and every
        % table grows by a blank line per row. Real floats reset that; a pinned
        % one has to be told.
        \usepackage{etoolbox}
        \AtBeginEnvironment{table}{\singlespacing}
        \AtBeginEnvironment{longtable}{\singlespacing}
        % Note under a figure, matching the "Notes:" block under the tables.
        \newcommand{\fignote}[1]{\par\vspace{-0.4\baselineskip}\begingroup
          \centering\begin{minipage}{0.92\linewidth}\footnotesize
          \setstretch{1.0}\noindent\emph{Notes:} #1\par\end{minipage}\par
          \endgroup\vspace{0.4\baselineskip}}
        % Table and figure lists, set like the table of contents.
        % Bare URLs set in the body face rather than typewriter, so the one
        % link in the appendix does not import a second font family.
        \AtBeginDocument{\urlstyle{same}}
        \renewcommand{\listtablename}{List of Tables}
        \renewcommand{\listfigurename}{List of Figures}
bibliography: references.bib
# Ley 26.075 appears only in the framework table, whose sources are plain text
# because a kableExtra note is raw LaTeX that pandoc never resolves. Without this
# it would drop out of the reference list.
nocite: |
  @ley26075_2005
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
  cache: false
---

```{r setup}
# The R session that knits this document may start in the C locale. When it does,
# knitr writes every non-ASCII character into the LaTeX as a literal "<U+00F3>"
# escape, so accented place names print as that string instead of as the letter.
# The bytes and the Encoding() tag are already correct; what is missing is a
# native encoding that can represent them. Set before anything is rendered.
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "en_US.UTF-8"))

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table); library(knitr); library(kableExtra)
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center", out.width = "92%", fig.pos = "H")
# Paths anchored to the project root via here (matches the analysis scripts).
TAB <- here::here("output", "tables"); FIG <- here::here("output", "figures")

# Read a saved table; NULL if not yet produced.
# fread returns character columns WITHOUT the UTF-8 encoding tag, so an accented
# value read from a committed table reaches LaTeX as raw bytes and xelatex draws
# two glyphs instead of one ("C<c3><b3>rdoba"). Tagging here fixes it once for
# every table rather than escaping accents by hand in each one.
read_out <- function(f) {
  p <- file.path(TAB, f)
  if (!file.exists(p)) return(NULL)
  d <- fread(p, encoding = "UTF-8")
  for (j in names(d)) if (is.character(d[[j]])) Encoding(d[[j]]) <- "UTF-8"
  d[]
}

# Render a saved table as a booktabs PDF table (placeholder note if missing).
# Appendix dumps are set at ONE declared size rather than scaled per table:
# scale_down gives every wide table its own arbitrary font size, which breaks the
# single-family typography the body and the figures share.
# A variable name is not a column heading, and it is not a row label either. The
# dumped tables used to carry the pipeline's own snake_case names into the PDF,
# in the header AND in the first column, which reads as an unfinished output.
# Renaming happens HERE so it applies to every dump at once and to any added
# later. Escaping stays ON, so the labels are plain text: a header carrying LaTeX
# would have to travel with escape = FALSE, and that turns every underscore
# elsewhere in the table into a subscript.
HEAD <- c(att = "ATT", se = "s.e.", p = "p-value", n = "N", n_obs = "N",
          n_units = "Units", n_sch = "Schools", n_schools = "Schools",
          ci_lo = "95% CI, lower", ci_hi = "95% CI, upper", k = "Lead/lag",
          att_pp = "ATT (pp)", se_pp = "s.e. (pp)",
          base_rate_pp = "Untreated mean (pp)", std_difference = "Std. difference",
          ever_treated = "Ever treated", never_treated = "Never treated",
          fect_att = "FEct ATT", fect_se = "FEct s.e.", pct_public = "State %",
          pct_rural = "Rural %", log_enroll = "Log enrolment",
          bl_ses = "Baseline SES", bl_score_lang = "Baseline language",
          bl_score_math = "Baseline mathematics", pretrend_f_p = "Pre-trend p-value",
          counterfactual_trend = "Counterfactual trend", n_units_used = "Units used")
prettify <- function(x) vapply(as.character(x), function(v) {
  if (is.na(v)) return(NA_character_)
  if (v %in% names(HEAD)) return(unname(HEAD[v]))
  if (!grepl("_", v)) return(v)                    # leave prose values alone
  v <- gsub("_", " ", v)
  v <- sub("^pct ", "", v)
  sub("^(.)", "\\U\\1", v, perl = TRUE)
}, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)

exhibit_tbl <- function(f, digits = 3, cols = NULL, dt = NULL, font_size = 9,
                        note = NULL, src = NULL) {
  d <- if (!is.null(dt)) dt else read_out(f)
  if (is.null(d)) return(kbl(data.frame(Status = paste("exhibit pending:", f)),
                             booktabs = TRUE, linesep = ""))
  if (!is.null(cols)) d <- d[, ..cols]
  d <- copy(d)
  for (j in names(d)) if (is.character(d[[j]])) set(d, j = j, value = prettify(d[[j]]))
  k <- kbl(d, booktabs = TRUE, digits = digits, linesep = "",
           col.names = prettify(names(d))) |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = font_size)
  if (is.null(note) && is.null(src)) return(k)
  tbl_note(k, if (is.null(note)) "" else note, src = src)
}

# Table note in the applied-micro convention: the word "Notes:" in italic, the
# note one size below the body, spanning the table width. Every results table
# declares estimator, treatment definition, comparison group, aggregation window
# and clustering here rather than in the prose, because notes do not count
# towards the word limit and the reader needs them beside the numbers.
# Notes carry what the reader needs beside the numbers; Sources carry where the
# non-estimated content came from. CITEKEYS CANNOT GO IN EITHER: this block is
# raw LaTeX that pandoc never sees, so `@key` would print literally (and its
# underscore starts math mode). Bibliographic sources belong in the caption,
# which pandoc does process; `src` is for plain-text provenance. They are separate blocks because a caption
# should name the table, not explain it, and a source is not a note.
tbl_note <- function(x, ..., src = NULL) {
  g <- paste0("\\\\emph{Notes:} ", paste0(..., collapse = ""))
  if (!is.null(src)) g <- c(g, paste0("\\\\emph{Sources:} ", src))
  footnote(x, general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE, general = g)
}

# Guarded figure include (placeholder text if missing).
exhibit_fig <- function(f) {
  p <- file.path(FIG, f)
  if (file.exists(p)) knitr::include_graphics(p)
  else knitr::asis_output(sprintf("\\emph{[figure pending: %s]}", f))
}

# ---- Key figures pulled from saved outputs (computed at render time) --------
.mr  <- read_out("01_match_rate_by_wave.csv")
.iv  <- read_out("11d_identifying_variation.csv")
.rev <- read_out("11_reversal_accounting.csv")
.ext <- read_out("03_extended_day_by_year.csv")
.ful <- read_out("03_full_day_by_year.csv")
.tr  <- read_out("09_trajectory_results.csv")
link_lo <- if (!is.null(.mr))  sprintf("%.1f", min(.mr$match_rate)) else "[n/a]"
link_hi <- if (!is.null(.mr))  sprintf("%.1f", max(.mr$match_rate)) else "[n/a]"
n_sch   <- if (!is.null(.iv))  format(.iv[metric == "schools"]$full,      big.mark = ",") else "[n/a]"
n_sw    <- if (!is.null(.iv))  format(.iv[metric == "school_waves"]$full, big.mark = ",") else "[n/a]"
rev_pct <- if (!is.null(.rev)) round(.rev[scope == "RA annual history (all schools)"]$pct_reverting) else "[n/a]"
readopt_pct <- if (!is.null(.rev)) round(.rev[scope == "RA annual history (all schools)"]$pct_readopting) else "[n/a]"
# Reversal read on either definition, and the size of any wave-dated cohort:
# both are quantities Appendix A turns on.
rv <- function(sc, col = "pct_reverting") if (!is.null(.rev))
  sprintf("%.1f", .rev[scope == sc][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
.csz <- read_out("11d_cohort_sizes.csv")
csz <- function(y) if (!is.null(.csz))
  fmtn(.csz[sample == "full" & cohort_year == y]$schools) else "[n/a]"

# ---- Empirical strategy: event time, switching and inference ---------------
.sw   <- read_out("03_switches_per_school.csv")
.hz   <- read_out("11d_switchers_by_horizon.csv")
.ecl  <- read_out("06j_exposure_classes.csv")
.eval <- read_out("06l_exposure_validity.csv")
.eff  <- read_out("06f_effective_clusters.csv")
.lopo <- read_out("06k_leave_one_province.csv")
.idg  <- read_out("06f_inference_diagnostics.csv")
.rsm  <- read_out("06f_resampling.csv")

fmtn <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
# Assessment calendar, read off the wave table rather than hard-coded.
n_waves  <- if (!is.null(.mr)) nrow(.mr) else "[n/a]"
wave_yrs <- if (!is.null(.mr)) sort(.mr$year) else NULL
wave_gaps <- if (!is.null(wave_yrs))
  knitr::combine_words(as.character(diff(wave_yrs)), and = " and ") else "[n/a]"
# Schools whose treatment switches two or more times: the design fact that rules
# out an absorbing-adoption estimator.
n_multi <- if (!is.null(.sw)) fmtn(.sw[switches >= 2, sum(schools)]) else "[n/a]"
# Switchers supporting each horizon, in the wave-indexed specification.
hz_n <- function(k) if (!is.null(.hz))
  fmtn(.hz[sample == "full" & trimws(horizon) == paste0("Effect_", k)]$switchers) else "[n/a]"
# Classes of calendar time since first adoption. 06j carries a `definition`
# column with the single value "main" -- it reported two until the persistence
# rule was retired -- so the filter below is kept rather than dropped.
.ecs <- if (!is.null(.ecl)) .ecl[definition == "main"] else NULL
exp_modal_pct <- if (!is.null(.ecs)) sprintf("%.0f", max(.ecs$pct)) else "[n/a]"
exp_top3_pct  <- if (!is.null(.ecs)) sprintf("%.0f", .ecs[exposure <= 2, sum(pct)]) else "[n/a]"
exp_max       <- if (!is.null(.ecs)) max(.ecs$exposure) else "[n/a]"
# How far calendar time since first adoption departs from years actually treated.
eval_pick <- function(h, e, col) if (!is.null(.eval))
  sprintf("%.0f", .eval[horizon == h & years_since_adoption == e][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
gap_h2_e1 <- eval_pick(2, 1, "pct_no_gap")
# Effective clusters and the leverage check on provinces.
eff_sw <- if (!is.null(.eff)) sprintf("%.1f", .eff[base == "switchers"]$effective_clusters) else "[n/a]"
n_prov <- if (!is.null(.eff)) .eff[base == "switchers"]$n_clusters else "[n/a]"
.lm <- if (!is.null(.lopo)) .lopo[subject == "mathematics" & dropped != "none (full sample)"] else NULL
lopo_lo <- if (!is.null(.lm)) sprintf("%.3f", min(.lm$att)) else "[n/a]"
lopo_hi <- if (!is.null(.lm)) sprintf("%.3f", max(.lm$att)) else "[n/a]"
# Calendar span of a unit of event time: the waves are not equally spaced, which
# is what makes a relative-magnitude bound uninterpretable on this event study.
wave_gap_lo <- if (!is.null(wave_yrs)) min(diff(wave_yrs)) else "[n/a]"
wave_gap_hi <- if (!is.null(wave_yrs)) max(diff(wave_yrs)) else "[n/a]"
# Smallest eigenvalue of the primary estimator's joint effects-and-placebos
# covariance matrix: negative, which is why no sensitivity method that needs a
# valid covariance matrix is run on it.
.ev <- if (!is.null(.idg)) .idg[diagnostic %like% "^vcov" & quantity %like% "^eigenvalue"] else NULL
min_eig <- if (!is.null(.ev)) sprintf("%.4f", min(as.numeric(.ev$value))) else "[n/a]"
# Province-clustered resampling inference, for the estimators that admit it.
rs <- function(est, subj, inf, col = "p", lv = "province") if (!is.null(.rsm))
  sprintf("%.3f", .rsm[estimator %like% est & subject == subj & cluster_level == lv &
                       inference %like% inf][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
# The primary estimator under each inference procedure. `cb` gives the standard
# error, `cbt` the ratio the SAME point estimate carries under that procedure —
# the quantity that moves, since the estimate itself does not.
.cdb <- read_out("06q_cdh_bootstrap.csv")
cb <- function(s, par, col = "se_boot_package") if (!is.null(.cdb))
  sprintf("%.3f", .cdb[subject == s & parameter == par][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
cbt <- function(s, par, col = "se_boot_package") if (!is.null(.cdb)) {
  r <- .cdb[subject == s & parameter == par]
  sprintf("%.2f", r$att / r[[col]]) } else "[n/a]"
# How general the province shrinkage is, counted rather than asserted: it is NOT
# every cell, and the exception matters enough that the count is read from the
# file instead of being described in words that could go stale.
shrink_n  <- if (!is.null(.cdb)) .cdb[se_province < se_school, .N] else "[n/a]"
shrink_of <- if (!is.null(.cdb)) nrow(.cdb) else "[n/a]"

# Share of primary schools in each regime, by year (Context).
pct <- function(d, y, col) if (!is.null(d)) sprintf("%.1f", d[year == y][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
# Same series, as a count rather than a share: how many primary schools clear the
# treatment threshold in a given year.
cnt <- function(d, y, col) if (!is.null(d)) fmtn(d[year == y][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
ext_11 <- pct(.ext, 2011, "has_regime_pct"); ful_11 <- pct(.ful, 2011, "has_regime_pct")
ext_22 <- pct(.ext, 2022, "has_regime_pct"); ext_23 <- pct(.ext, 2023, "has_regime_pct")
ext_25 <- pct(.ext, 2025, "has_regime_pct"); ful_22 <- pct(.ful, 2022, "has_regime_pct")
ful_23 <- pct(.ful, 2023, "has_regime_pct"); ful_25 <- pct(.ful, 2025, "has_regime_pct")
ext100_22 <- pct(.ext, 2022, "share_eq_100_pct"); ext100_23 <- pct(.ext, 2023, "share_eq_100_pct")
# State-managed share among ever- and never-treated schools: the federal
# federal programme is offered only to this sector, so the composition
# of the two groups by management is a scope condition rather than a covariate.
.bal <- read_out("03_baseline_balance.csv")
pub <- function(col) if (!is.null(.bal))
  sprintf("%.0f", 100 * .bal[variable == "pct_public"][[col]]) else "[n/a]"

# Assessment coverage: Aprender reaches ~2/3 of primary schools, and the ones it
# misses are much smaller and far less often treated (Data, sources and linkage).
.cov <- read_out("03_assessment_coverage.csv")
cv <- function(m) if (!is.null(.cov)) .cov[metric == m]$value else NA_real_
cov_pct  <- if (!is.null(.cov)) sprintf("%.0f", 100 * cv("schools with at least one Aprender score") /
                                          cv("primary schools in the RA census (ever)")) else "[n/a]"
n_prim   <- if (!is.null(.cov)) format(cv("primary schools in the RA census (ever)"), big.mark = ",") else "[n/a]"
med_in   <- if (!is.null(.cov)) cv("median primary enrolment, assessed")     else "[n/a]"
med_out  <- if (!is.null(.cov)) cv("median primary enrolment, not assessed") else "[n/a]"
trt_in   <- if (!is.null(.cov)) cv("% treated (share >= 50%), assessed")     else "[n/a]"
trt_out  <- if (!is.null(.cov)) cv("% treated (share >= 50%), not assessed") else "[n/a]"
bal_pct  <- if (!is.null(.cov)) cv("% of estimation-panel schools present in all six waves") else "[n/a]"
bal5_pct <- if (!is.null(.cov)) cv("% of estimation-panel schools present in all five census waves") else "[n/a]"
# Schools assessed in the 2022 sample wave, against a census wave, from the match
# table: the contrast is what makes the six-wave figure a design fact.
n22   <- if (!is.null(.mr)) fmtn(.mr[year == 2022]$schools) else "[n/a]"
ncens <- if (!is.null(.mr)) fmtn(round(mean(.mr[wave_type == "census"]$schools), -2)) else "[n/a]"

# ---- Results: the rollout, the measurement correction, the estimates --------
.coh  <- read_out("03_adoption_cohorts.csv")
.tt   <- read_out("03_treatment_transitions.csv")
.rh   <- read_out("08b_recording_by_hours.csv")
.rp   <- read_out("08b_recording_by_province.csv")
.fhm  <- read_out("08b_five_hour_margin.csv")
.hbs  <- read_out("08b_hours_by_sector.csv")
# Reported hours by management sector: the two sectors run under different rules
# and the federal programme reaches only one of them.
hbs <- function(y, sec, col = "mean_hours") if (!is.null(.hbs))
  sprintf(if (col == "mean_hours") "%.2f" else "%.1f",
          .hbs[year == y & sector == sec][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
.lrl  <- read_out("08b_labelling_rule.csv")
# What the school-level labelling rule does to the arms. Not to the shares: those
# are computed from each wave's own reported hours.
lr <- function(q) if (!is.null(.lrl))
  format(.lrl[quantity == q]$value, big.mark = ",") else "[n/a]"
.cont <- read_out("08_contamination_2023.csv")
.arm  <- read_out("08_arm_results.csv")
.hs   <- read_out("06g_horizon_sensitivity.csv")
.mp   <- read_out("06g_max_placebos.csv")
.opt  <- read_out("06g_cdh_options.csv")
.pl   <- read_out("06_placebos.csv")
.m    <- read_out("06_estimation_main.csv")
.pj   <- read_out("06j_exposure_partition.csv")
.lf   <- read_out("11b_like_for_like.csv")

# Adoption cohorts, by the calendar year the school first crosses the threshold.
coh <- function(y, col = "schools") if (!is.null(.coh)) fmtn(.coh[cohort == y][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
# Wave-to-wave transitions, as a share of school-wave transitions.
tt <- function(dir) if (!is.null(.tt)) sprintf("%.2f", .tt[direction == dir]$pct) else "[n/a]"

# Recording rate: of the schools whose directors report a given length of day,
# the share the census records as extended. `rec` is comparable across waves;
# `rec23` uses the finer 2023 categories.
rec   <- function(y, h) if (!is.null(.rh))
  sprintf("%.1f", .rh[scale == "comparable across waves" & year == y & hours == h]$rate_pct) else "[n/a]"
rec23 <- function(h) if (!is.null(.rh))
  sprintf("%.1f", .rh[scale == "2023 detail" & hours == h]$rate_pct) else "[n/a]"
nrec  <- function(y, h) if (!is.null(.rh))
  fmtn(.rh[scale == "comparable across waves" & year == y & hours == h]$schools) else "[n/a]"
fhm   <- function(q) if (!is.null(.fhm)) {
  v <- .fhm[quantity == q]$value; if (v >= 100) fmtn(v) else sprintf("%.1f", v) } else "[n/a]"
# Six-hour recording across jurisdictions in 2021, before the federal programme.
.p21 <- if (!is.null(.rp)) .rp[cut == "2021, 6h or more" & rated == TRUE] else NULL
p21_n   <- if (!is.null(.p21)) nrow(.p21) else "[n/a]"
p21_out <- if (!is.null(.p21)) .p21[which.min(rate_pct)] else NULL
p21_lo  <- if (!is.null(.p21)) sprintf("%.0f", min(.p21[rate_pct > p21_out$rate_pct]$rate_pct)) else "[n/a]"
p21_hi  <- if (!is.null(.p21)) sprintf("%.0f", max(.p21$rate_pct)) else "[n/a]"

# Composition of what the census calls extended day in 2023, stock against flow.
ctm <- function(w, cls) if (!is.null(.cont)) {
  r <- .cont[when == w]; sprintf("%.1f", 100 * r[[cls]] / sum(r$genuine, r$horamas, r$none)) } else "[n/a]"
ctm_n <- function(w) if (!is.null(.cont)) {
  r <- .cont[when == w]; fmtn(sum(r$genuine, r$horamas, r$none)) } else "[n/a]"
# Treatment-arm estimates.
arm <- function(a, s, col = "att") if (!is.null(.arm))
  sprintf("%.3f", .arm[estimator == "CDH" & arm == a & subject == s][[col]]) else "[n/a]"

# The pooled estimator under each aggregation window, and its own placebo. The
# regime argument selects the treatment arm: combined, or full day alone.
hz <- function(n, s, par = "ATE", col = "estimate", rg = "combined") if (!is.null(.hs)) {
  r <- .hs[regime == rg & spec == paste0(n, " horizon(s)") & subject == s & parameter == par]
  if (col == "t") sprintf("%.2f", r$estimate / r$se) else sprintf("%.3f", r[[col]]) } else "[n/a]"
# Both placebos the main specification admits, which the horizon above does
# not report: it holds the placebo at one so that only the window varies. These
# are the SAME estimates as the k = -1 and k = -2 leads of the event study, which
# 06g asserts; the two exhibits are one diagnostic and never corroborate one
# another.
mp <- function(s, par = "Placebo_1", col = "estimate", rg = "combined") if (!is.null(.mp)) {
  r <- .mp[regime == rg & subject == s & parameter == par]
  if (col == "t") sprintf("%.2f", r$estimate / r$se) else sprintf("%.3f", r[[col]]) } else "[n/a]"
# Aggregation window of the exposure classes, in ONE place. It has to match the
# window of the pooled row the classes are read against -- `effects = 2` in
# 06_estimation.R -- because @tbl-main sets the three classes directly underneath
# that row and @tbl-timing-placebo pairs each with its own placebo. 06j saves four
# windows per class, so a filter naming the wrong one returns a full set of
# plausible numbers estimated on a different aggregation, and nothing errors. The
# literal used to be typed three times (here and in the two chunks below) with
# nothing tying them together, which is the same undeclared-invariant problem the
# pipeline hit with the duplicated treatment definition.
PJ_WINDOW <- "2 horizons"
# An empty filter is the failure mode this constant exists to prevent, and it is
# silent: sprintf() on a zero-row selection prints nothing rather than failing.
if (!is.null(.pj) && !PJ_WINDOW %in% .pj$spec)
  stop("PJ_WINDOW (", PJ_WINDOW, ") is not a `spec` in 06j_exposure_partition.csv; ",
       "available: ", paste(unique(.pj$spec), collapse = " | "))

# Exposure classes: estimate, standard error and placebo of each class.
pj <- function(x, s, par = "ATE", col = "estimate", sp = PJ_WINDOW) if (!is.null(.pj)) {
  r <- .pj[definition == "main" & spec == sp & exposure_years == x &
           subject == s & parameter == par]
  if (col == "t") sprintf("%.2f", r$estimate / r$se) else sprintf("%.3f", r[[col]]) } else "[n/a]"
# Options the primary estimator exposes: fixed switcher sets, own trends, controls.
opt <- function(sp, s, par = "ATE", col = "estimate") if (!is.null(.opt)) {
  r <- .opt[spec == sp & subject == s & parameter == par]
  if (col == "t") sprintf("%.2f", r$estimate / r$se) else sprintf("%.3f", r[[col]]) } else "[n/a]"
# Estimation grid: any row of the main specification table.
# Union of the 95% intervals across estimator families on the common sample: the
# widest claim the evidence permits, computed rather than quoted, because it moves
# whenever any family does.
uni <- function(side) if (!is.null(.lf)) sprintf("%.2f",
  if (side == "lo") min(.lf$att - 1.96 * .lf$se) else max(.lf$att + 1.96 * .lf$se)) else "[n/a]"
mn <- function(e, s, col = "att", reg = "combined", cov = "none (absorbed)") if (!is.null(.m))
  sprintf("%.3f", .m[estimator == e & regime == reg & subject == s & covariates == cov][[col]]) else "[n/a]"

# ---- Parallel trends, and why the estimators disagree -----------------------
.es   <- read_out("07_event_study_cdh.csv")
.esc  <- read_out("07_event_study_cs_covariates.csv")
.esx  <- read_out("07_event_study_cdh_controls.csv")

# Event studies. `es` is the primary estimator, `esc` the doubly-robust one,
# which is read only over its pre-treatment window (see the appendix).

# resolve to the column of the same name and match every row.
es  <- function(kk, s, col = "est") if (!is.null(.es))
  sprintf("%.3f", .es[spec == "uncontrolled" & subject == s & k == kk][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
esc <- function(kk, s, col = "est", sp = "uncontrolled") if (!is.null(.esc))
  sprintf("%.3f", .esc[spec == sp & subject == s & k == kk][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
# The same lead under the primary estimator with contemporaneous composition controls.
esx <- function(kk, s, sp = "uncontrolled", col = "est") if (!is.null(.esx))
  sprintf("%.3f", .esx[spec == sp & subject == s & k == kk][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
# Outcome scale: the same placebo under the anchored and the within-wave scale.
sc  <- function(s, sk, col = "k2") if (!is.null(.sc))
  sprintf("%.3f", .sc[subject == s & scale == sk][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
# The k = -2 mathematics placebo by region, and by adoption cohort.

  sprintf("%.3f", .reg[region == r][[col]]) else "[n/a]"

  sprintf("%.3f", .cd[k == -2 & subject == s & g_year == gy][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
# Placebo of any specification of the primary estimator. `k` selects which one:
# the design admits as many placebos as horizons, and for the headline it is the
# SECOND that rejects, so a helper that silently returned the first would clear
# specifications on half their pre-treatment evidence.
plc <- function(e, rg, s, col = "att", k = 1) if (!is.null(.pl))
  sprintf("%.3f", .pl[estimator == e & regime == rg & subject == s &
                      placebo == paste0("Placebo_", k)][[col]]) else "[n/a]"

# The imputation estimator, its pre-treatment tests and the two refuted stories.
fct <- function(e, s, col = "att") if (!is.null(.fe))
  sprintf("%.3f", .fe[estimator == e & subject == s][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
ft  <- function(sp, col) if (!is.null(.ft)) {
  v <- .ft[spec == sp][[col]]; if (v < 0.001) format(v, digits = 2, scientific = TRUE)
  else sprintf("%.3f", v) } else "[n/a]"
co  <- function(s, sp) if (!is.null(.co))
  sprintf("%.3f", .co[subject == s & spec == sp]$att) else "[n/a]"
nr  <- function(e, s, col = "att") if (!is.null(.nr))
  sprintf("%.3f", .nr[estimator == e & subject == s][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
# Wave and cohort composition, and the pre-trend test on each sample.
cvr <- function(sp, col) if (!is.null(.cvr)) sprintf("%.3f", .cvr[spec == sp][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
sg  <- function(sm, s, col = "fect_att") if (!is.null(.sg)) {
  v <- .sg[sample == sm & subject == s][[col]]
  if (col == "pretrend_f_p" && v < 0.001) format(v, digits = 2, scientific = TRUE)
  else sprintf("%.3f", v) } else "[n/a]"
# Identifying variation retained when the 2023 cohort is excluded, overall and
# among the switchers that support each horizon.
ivr <- function(m) if (!is.null(.iv)) sprintf("%.0f", .iv[metric == m]$pct_retained) else "[n/a]"
hz_ret <- function(k) if (!is.null(.hz)) {
  g <- function(sm) .hz[sample == sm & trimws(horizon) == paste0("Effect_", k)]$switchers
  sprintf("%.0f", 100 * g("excl. 2023 cohort") / g("full")) } else "[n/a]"
# Estimators on the common sample of Panel B.
lf  <- function(e, s, col = "att") if (!is.null(.lf))
  sprintf("%.3f", .lf[estimator == e & subject == s][[col]]) else "[n/a]"

  sprintf("%.3f", .het[dimension == dm & group == gp & subject == s & sample == sm][[col]]) else "[n/a]"

  fmtn(.het[dimension == dm & group == gp & subject == s & sample == sm]$sw1) else "[n/a]"

.th <- read_out("04_threshold_sensitivity_cdh.csv")
# Small counts are spelled out in the prose, so an inline count has to be a word
# rather than a digit; anything above the range the manuscript ever cites falls
# back to the numeral instead of failing silently.
num_word <- function(n) {
  w <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")
  if (is.na(n) || n < 1 || n > length(w)) as.character(n) else w[n]
}
# Constructions of the binary indicator compared in @tbl-rob-treatdef.
n_treatdef <- if (!is.null(.th)) num_word(uniqueN(.th$threshold)) else "[n/a]"

# Rambachan--Roth: the relative-magnitude bound at which a specification's robust
# confidence set first covers zero. Read from each specification's own file rather
# than stated once for all four, because it is NOT the same in all four: three
# cover zero at the smallest bound the method was run at and one does not, so a
# single typed number would misreport a quarter of the exhibit.
HD_SPECS <- list(c("language", "uncontrolled"), c("language", "baselinecovariates"),
                 c("mathematics", "uncontrolled"), c("mathematics", "baselinecovariates"))
hd <- function(s, sp) read_out(sprintf("07_honestdid_%s_%s.csv", s, sp))
hd_zero <- function(s, sp = "uncontrolled") {
  d <- hd(s, sp); if (is.null(d)) return("[n/a]")
  z <- d[lb <= 0 & ub >= 0]
  # The value is set inside $...$ in the text, so the no-coverage case returns
  # LaTeX maths (">2") rather than the words "more than 2.0", which would be set
  # as italic variables and spaced as a product.
  if (!nrow(z)) sprintf("> %.1f", max(d$Mbar)) else sprintf("%.1f", min(z$Mbar))
}
# How many of the four cover zero at a given bound, counted rather than asserted.
hd_n_at <- function(m = 0.5) sum(vapply(HD_SPECS, function(k) {
  d <- hd(k[1], k[2])
  !is.null(d) && nrow(d[abs(Mbar - m) < 1e-9 & lb <= 0 & ub >= 0]) > 0
}, logical(1)))
.ga <- read_out("06e_grade_alignment.csv")
.g6 <- read_out("06e_g6_certain_bound.csv")

  sprintf("%.0f", (if (is.null(y)) .g6[is.na(year)] else .g6[year == y])$pct_certain) else "[n/a]"

# The treatment-definition grid, and the grade-6-certain restriction.
th <- function(tr, s, col = "att") if (!is.null(.th))
  sprintf("%.3f", .th[threshold == tr & subject == s][[col]]) else "[n/a]"
ga <- function(sm, s) if (!is.null(.ga))
  sprintf("%.3f", .ga[sample == sm & subject == s]$att) else "[n/a]"
# The outcome under the anchored and the within-wave scale.

  sprintf("%.3f", .sc[subject == s & scale == sk]$att) else "[n/a]"

# Grade non-promotion: effect, interval and the level it is measured against, so

# CITED, not estimated: the only number in this chunk that does not come from a
# committed output. It is the headline of Nistal (2022) -- a 23.1%
# reduction in non-promotion -- rescaled below onto the untreated mean of THIS
# panel so their relative effect can be read against the interval estimated here.
EN_REDUCTION <- 0.231
.np <- if (!is.null(.tr)) .tr[outcome == "nonpromotion" & spec == "CDH full panel"] else NULL
np_att  <- if (!is.null(.np)) sprintf("%.2f", .np$att_pp) else "[n/a]"
np_lo   <- if (!is.null(.np)) sprintf("%.2f", .np$att_pp - 1.96 * .np$se_pp) else "[n/a]"
np_hi   <- if (!is.null(.np)) sprintf("%.2f", .np$att_pp + 1.96 * .np$se_pp) else "[n/a]"
np_base <- if (!is.null(.np)) sprintf("%.1f", .np$base_rate_pp) else "[n/a]"
np_en   <- if (!is.null(.np)) sprintf("%.2f", EN_REDUCTION * .np$base_rate_pp) else "[n/a]"
```

# Abstract {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```{=latex}
\begin{spacing}{1.15}\noindent
```
Does expanding the school day raise student achievement in Argentine primary education, and for whom? This dissertation links the annual school census (*Relevamiento Anual*, 2011–2025) to six waves of the *Aprender* assessment (2016–2025) in a school-level staggered difference-in-differences design. Two features of the setting shape identification. First, the administrative extended-day category does not cleanly distinguish genuine six-hour extension from the five-hour day introduced under the federal 1h+ programme: the 2023 adoption flow is predominantly five-hour, and classification varies sharply across jurisdictions. Second, treatment is markedly non-absorbing — about 47% of ever-treated schools later contract — requiring an estimator that accommodates repeated treatment changes. The assessment calendar creates an additional problem: event time measured in waves pools schools observed at different calendar distances from their first switch. Partitioning by that timing shows that the positive mathematics estimate is concentrated among schools assessed in their adoption year, where a pre-treatment placebo is of comparable magnitude. Estimator families also disagree over the counterfactual trend; the large 2023 cohort explains much of the pre-treatment divergence and the disagreement in language, but not the remaining dispersion in mathematics. Overall, the data do not provide robustly identified evidence that longer school days raised grade-6 achievement. Estimates are larger in more disadvantaged schools, but the heterogeneity evidence remains exploratory. The effect is not identified as zero: intervals still contain policy-relevant effects in either direction.

# Introduction

When policymakers ask how to raise student achievement in unequal school systems, and especially how to raise it for the most disadvantaged, one answer recurs: give children more time in school. Lengthening the school day has featured in reforms across Europe, Latin America and the United States, [@patall2010; @oecd2021], and it promises three things at once: more hours of instruction [@carroll1963]; a more even distribution of opportunity, since school may compensate for home disadvantage [@cooper1996; @alexander2007; @quinn2016]; and, for families in precarious circumstances, care for children and the working hours it releases for their parents [@berthelon2011; @oecd2021]. The political case rarely separates the three while this dissertation measures only the first.

Argentina has committed to that answer on paper for two decades. National law has required every primary school to be of extended day (more than 4 hours) or full day (8 hours) for two decades since 2026 [@len2006], against a traditional four-hour day, and successive federal resolutions have renewed the goal [@cfe426_2022; @cfe470_2024]. Delivery has not followed: in 2025, the last year of the school census, `r cnt(.ext, 2025, "share_ge_50")` primary schools clear the threshold used here, `r pct(.ext, 2025, "share_ge_50_pct")`% of the total. The intended purpose of the additional hours is also explicit: the 2022 resolution assigns them primarly to written production, reading comprehension and mathematical literacy [@cfe426_2022], while 2024 amendment restates the objective as intensifying the teaching of mathematics and language [@cfe470_2024]. These are the two domains measured by *Aprender*, Argentina's national assessment of primary pupils. Whether the longer school day improved them remains an open empirical question, and it is the question this dissertation tackles.

The dissertation links Argentina's national administrative sources relevant to this question — the annual school census (*Relevamiento Anual*, RA) and the *Aprender* assessments — into a school-level panel of `r n_sw` school-waves contributed by `r n_sch` distinct primary schools, unbalanced because not every school is assessed in every wave. *Aprender* provides six waves in which both mathematics and language are tested: 2016, 2018, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2025. Using this panel, the dissertation estimates the effect of extended- and full-day schooling on sixth-grade student achievement[^terms] in mathematics and language with a staggered difference-in-differences design. One feature of the setting determines the choice of estimator: schools do not adopt the longer day once and for all, but move in and out of it. Treatment is therefore non-absorbing, requiring an estimator that accommodates reapeated treatment changes and effects that vary across schools and over time [@dechaisemartindyn2026].

[^terms]: Student achievement and test scores are used interchangeably to denote this measured construct, following OECD usage [@oecd_pisa2022].

First, this dissertation shows that the census category used to track expansion does not cleanly distinguish genuine six-hour extension from the five-hour day introduced under the federal programme (*1h+*), and the resulting misclassification varies sharply across jurisdictions. The treatment process creates a second complication. Schools move into and out of the longer-day regime rather than adopting it permanently, so the analysis requires estimators that accommodate non-absorbing treatment and heterogeneous effects. These estimators do not deliver a common answer. The disagreement is itself informative: diagnostics locate much of the pre-treatment divergence and the disagreement in language in the large 2023 adoption cohort, while the remaining dispersion in mathematics is partly associated with differences in the populations the estimators weight. Taken together, the evidence does not provide a robustly identified positive effect of longer-day schooling on achievement. The closest Argentine antecedent, [@edonistal2022], instead studies grade retention across primary schooling (Appendix C relates that broader trajectory outcome to the grade-6 outcomes examined here).

The remainder of this study proceeds as follows. @sec-lit reviews the theoretical framework and empirical evidence on instructional time and the distribution of its gains. @sec-context describes the setting. @sec-data presents the data, its linkage, and the construction of treatment and outcome; @sec-strategy, the research design; @sec-results reports the results, while @sec-robustness sets out the robustness, sensitivity, and diagnostic analyses. Finally, @sec-discussion discusses the study's limitations, implications, and concluding remarks.

# Literature review {#sec-lit}

The case for more time is direct — more hours in school should produce more learning — but it rests on a chain of assumptions the evidence does not uniformly support. This section takes the chain apart in the order the design depends on it: whether instructional time raises achievement at all, what the regional evidence says about how much, and a distributional question more consequential than the average effect — whether additional time compounds the inequalities children bring to school or offsets them.

## Instructional time as an input to learning {#sec-lit-time}

Instructional time is one input in an education production function whose marginal product need not be large or constant — a framing that traces back to @carroll1963, for whom achievement is a function of the time a student spends on a task relative to the time the task requires. Estimates that exploit within-student variation in time across subjects, which nets out school and student selection, find that additional instructional time does raise achievement, but that the effect is modest and contingent on how that time is used [@lavy2015; @rivkin2015]. @bietenbeck2023 revisit that evidence and find effects consistently smaller than earlier work implied. A regional synthesis reaches a compatible conclusion: because school days in Latin America and the Caribbean have historically been short, extension is plausibly high-return, but only where the added hours are well used [@holland2015]. That conditionality is the general lesson of the impact-evaluation literature in low- and middle-income countries, where additional resources raise achievement only when they change what children experience in the classroom [@ganimian2016]. More time is thus a necessary condition for more time-on-task, not a sufficient condition for higher achievement.

One qualification cuts the other way, and it governs how a null should be read here. If returns to time diminish, the extra hour buys most where the starting day is shortest — and the estimates above come from systems whose days were already long, while Argentina's *jornada simple* is a four-hour shift day. The prior for this setting is therefore favourable, which is what would make a null informative rather than expected. The closest institutional parallel bears that out: @orkin2013 studies Ethiopia's 2005 abolition of shift teaching in favour of a six-hour day and finds substantially larger gains, though on ordinal measures not comparable in magnitude.

## Latin American evidence and the distribution of gains {#sec-lit-latam}

Quasi-experimental work on regional reforms has tried to move from this prior to policy-specific estimates, and does not speak with one voice. The positive estimates are real but small, between 0.05 and 0.11 standard deviations across Chile, Colombia and Mexico [@bellei2009; @hincapie2016; @cabrera2019]. A random-effects meta-analysis of fourteen studies across eight countries — not including Argentina — puts the pooled primary-level effect at 0.04 standard deviations in both subjects [@alvarez2019]. That benchmark is small, so a design must resolve a few hundredths of a standard deviation to be informative, and fragile: the pooled mathematics estimate is significant only at the 10% level, and individual estimates run from $-0.22$ for Brazil's *Mais Educação* to $+0.29$ for Uruguay, averaging over programmes that did different things.

Others are more sceptical still: @arzola2011 finds Chile's full-day effect "small and not significant" under either definition of exposure, and a critical review of the Colombian evidence concludes the regional estimates are marginal, frequently insignificant and occasionally negative [@ramirez2019]. Nor is the ordering across subjects consistent.

The distributional question is sharper, and the evidence conflicts. @hincapie2016 finds the largest gains in poorer, rural schools, and @cabrera2019 also finds them concentrated there — though quantile estimates show the lowest-performing schools do not benefit at all, and richer schools spend the extra time on non-core subjects, a mechanism for why more time need not become more learning. @bellei2009 finds larger effects among rural and public-sector pupils but also in the upper part of the achievement distribution. One study points the other way: additional school days in Mexico raise performance only slightly, and least in poorer schools [@aguero2013]. This is a modern form of the hypothesis that schooling compensates for home disadvantage [@cooper1996; @alexander2007], whose magnitude recent work questions [@quinn2016], and whether extra time compresses or widens socioeconomic gaps carries opposite implications for a policy justified in the name of equity.

Two features of this literature govern how a null should be read, and both return in @sec-discussion. Extension is expensive and regional reviews judge it less cost-effective than the alternatives [@orkin2013; @holland2015; @contreras2023], so a null is informative rather than merely inconclusive [@arzola2011]. And whether an adopted programme is *sustained* is an open empirical question, yet the literature evaluates these reforms as though adoption were permanent.

## The Argentine evidence and its identification {#sec-lit-arg}

For a policy this large and this long-running, Argentine causal evidence on student achievement is thin. The most-cited antecedent exploits a single-city natural experiment that predates the current national framework, and finds enduring effects on educational attainment [@llach2009]. The closest modern study uses national administrative data for 2011–2019 and a two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences design, finding that lengthening the day reduces grade retention across primary schooling by 23% [@edonistal2022] — an effect on trajectories rather than on measured achievement, estimated over a window that closes before the largest phase of the policy.

That gap is empirical and methodological at once. The Argentine antecedent and much of the regional literature rely on two-way or cohort fixed-effects regressions, as does the closest institutional parallel, the Ethiopian shift-abolition study, whose districts also adopted at different times [@orkin2013]; the concern is therefore general to this literature rather than particular to Argentina. Under staggered adoption and heterogeneous effects, such estimators can be biased by "forbidden" comparisons that use already-treated units as controls [@dechaisemartin2020; @callaway2021; @goodmanbacon2021]. Two features of the Argentine setting bear on that concern. Extended-day status is non-absorbing — schools adopt the longer day and later revert, violating the assumption on which the standard staggered estimators rest — and the administrative "extended-day" category conflates genuine extension with a five-hour day introduced under a separate federal programme, so measured adoption overstates the treatment of interest.

## Contribution and research question {#sec-lit-rq}

Two moves position this dissertation against that literature, and the questions follow from them rather than sitting beside them.

The first problematises the measure that the literature and the policy both rely on. Every estimate of this reform, regional and Argentine alike, takes the administrative record of an extended day at face value. Here that record is shown to conflate genuine extension with a five-hour day funded under the same federal programme, so part of what the aggregate statistics count as expansion is a thinner intervention — a correction to the measure rather than a robustness check on an estimate.

The second problematises the identification. Prior work on this policy assumes adoption is permanent. It is not, and an estimator that assumes it discards the feature that most distinguishes this case — so establishing why estimator families disagree here is the warrant for the answer rather than an appendix to it.

The dissertation therefore asks: *does the expansion of extended- and full-day schooling in Argentine primary education improve grade-6 achievement in mathematics and language?* Because credibility depends on both moves, that question is inseparable from a second: *does the estimated effect survive once treatment reversal and the measurement of genuine extension are taken seriously, and once heterogeneity-robust estimators replace two-way fixed effects?* And in light of the region's unresolved distributional debate, a sub-question asks *for whom*: whether any effect differs across the socioeconomic distribution of schools. Variation by region and by treatment intensity is reported as supporting evidence rather than as a separate question, because neither rests on enough identifying variation to carry a causal reading.

# Context {#sec-context}

Argentine primary education is historically a half-day system. In the traditional *jornada simple*, children attend for 4 hours a day, in a morning or afternoon shift, with a single building often serving two separate cohorts [@edonistal2022]. Extending that day has been national policy for two decades, full day understood as roughly 8 hours and extended day as more than four but fewer than eight. @tbl-framework sets out the five instruments that establish it and what each contributes to this design.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-framework
#| tbl-cap: "Legal and programmatic framework of the longer school day."
# Built inline: normative facts with their own citations, not estimates. The
# citations live in the caption because a kableExtra note is raw LaTeX that
# pandoc never sees, so a citekey placed there would print literally.
fw <- data.table(
  Instrument = c("Ley 26.075", "Ley 26.206", "CFE 426/22", "RM 1765/22", "CFE 470/24"),
  Year = c("2005", "2006", "2022", "2022", "2024"),
  `What it establishes` = c(
    "Interim target: an extended- or full-day offer reaching 30 per cent of basic-education pupils by 2010",
    "Primary schooling \\emph{shall be} extended or full day (art.~28); national and provincial responsibility is joint and concurrent (art.~12); creates the Consejo Federal de Educaci\\'on (art.~116); common curricular content and priority learning cores (art.~85); primary education is a single pedagogical and organisational unit, compulsory from age six (art.~26); each jurisdiction chooses six years of primary plus six of secondary, or seven plus five (art.~134)",
    "Jurisdictions commit either to universalise the full or extended day, or to reach a minimum of 25 weekly hours",
    "Ministerial programme, known publicly as \\emph{1h+}, funding two routes of its routes in state-managed simple-day schools: an extended day of 10 additional weekly hours, and a fifth hour of five",
    "Targeted extension for lower-performing pupils; restates the aim as intensifying the teaching of mathematics and language"),
  `Bearing on this design` = c(
    "First quantified commitment against which coverage is reported",

    "Creates the five-hour route that the census records as extended day",
    "The intervention whose two modalities the census cannot separate",
    "The stated purpose maps onto the two domains \\emph{Aprender} measures"))
kbl(fw, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", escape = FALSE, align = c("l", "c", "l", "l")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 8) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "1.8cm") |> column_spec(3, width = "6.3cm") |>
  column_spec(4, width = "4.4cm") |>
  tbl_note("Article numbers refer to Ley 26.206.",
    src = paste0("Congreso de la Nación Argentina 2005, 2006; Consejo Federal de ",
```
