
Neither law is self-executing, and the reason is structural. Argentina is federal: responsibility for education is concurrent between the national state, the provinces and the Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires [@len2006]. The 24 jurisdictions own the buildings, employ the teachers and set the calendar, while the curricular content common to the whole country is agreed federally — so the curriculum *Aprender* measures against is not provincially defined. Extension therefore proceeds province by province and school by school, conditioned by classroom capacity, teacher supply and the cost of a second daily meal, some provinces having mandated the longer day before the national law and others having barely begun [@veleda2022] (@fig-provincial-timing). That decentralised rollout generates the staggered adoption exploited in @sec-strategy, and it means the schools able to adopt are not a random sample, which the identifying assumptions must confront rather than assume away. How a school comes to be treated follows from the same structure. The instruments fund and target the longer day (@tbl-framework), but the terms are settled in bilateral agreements that fix the number of schools reached rather than naming them [@rm1765_2022]. Which schools a province selects within that quota is set out in neither instrument. 

Adoption is therefore neither a school's own decision nor a national one, and the selection that matters is unobserved. The system also divides by management. State schools run the schedule their jurisdiction sets, which often does not follow the national commitment (@tbl-provincias); private schools set their own, with the provincial rule a floor rather than a timetable [@len2006], so they may run longer than it requires but not shorter. The directors' reported hours show both halves of that arrangement. Before the federal programme, in 2021, the private sector ran the longer day — a mean of `r hbs(2021, "private")` hours against `r hbs(2021, "public")` in the state sector, with `r hbs(2021, "private", "pct_4h_or_less")`% of private schools at 4 hours or less against `r hbs(2021, "public", "pct_4h_or_less")`% of state ones. By 2023 the ordering has reversed, to `r hbs(2023, "public")` hours against `r hbs(2023, "private")`. The programme funds only state-managed schools running a simple day [@unahoramas], so it moved the sector it pays for and left the other where it was, which is also why adoption is concentrated there: `r pub("ever_treated")`% of schools that ever cross the treatment threshold are state-managed, against `r pub("never_treated")`% of those that never do (@tbl-balance). @tbl-jurisdictions describes the systems that decision lands on, and they are not comparable units: the largest jurisdiction holds two orders of magnitude more primary schools than the smallest, and they differ as much in how rural, how state-managed and how large their schools are.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-jurisdictions
#| tbl-cap: "The 24 jurisdictions."
.jp <- read_out("03_jurisdiction_profile.csv")
if (!is.null(.jp)) {
  z <- .jp[order(-schools_last)]
  tab <- data.table(z$province, fmtn(z$schools_last),
                    sprintf("%.0f", z$pct_state), sprintf("%.0f", z$pct_rural),
                    sprintf("%.0f", z$median_size),
                    sprintf("%.1f", z$pct_treated_first),
                    sprintf("%.1f", z$pct_treated_last),
                    sprintf("%.0f", z$pct_assessed))
  kbl(tab, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", escape = FALSE,
      align = c("l", rep("r", 7)),
      col.names = c("Jurisdiction", "Schools", "State \\%", "Rural \\%",
                    "Median size", "Treated \\%, 2011", "Treated \\%, 2025",
                    "Assessed \\%")) |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 8) |>
    tbl_note(paste0(
      "Annual school census, 2025. The treated shares are given at both ends of the ",
      "panel to show the movement. \\\\emph{Assessed} is the share of schools ever ",
      "recorded as primary in the census that sit at least one \\\\emph{Aprender} wave; ",
      "it is what makes the estimand local to the schools the assessment reaches."))
} else exhibit_tbl("03_jurisdiction_profile.csv")
```


One feature of that structure bears directly on how treatment is measured. Each jurisdiction chooses between six years of primary followed by six of secondary and seven followed by five, so grade 6 is the final year of primary in some provinces and the second-to-last in others; and the census records the longer day for the cycle as a whole rather than for any one grade, which is why treatment is built over grades 1 to 7 (@sec-data-treat).

Implementation has fallen short of the commitments, and unevenly: in 2019 only 14.1% of primary pupils attended for more than 4 hours a day, with the jurisdictions ranging over the whole interval between [@veleda2022]. The census panel assembled here adds the feature that matters for what follows: the extended-day share was flat for the six years to 2022 and then doubled in a single year, to `r ext_23`% in 2023, while the share of schools running the extended day for their *entire* primary enrolment rose from `r ext100_22`% to `r ext100_23`% and the full-day share moved only to `r ful_23`%. The organisational change a genuine extension requires does not reach a tenth of the country's primary schools in twelve months.

This context matters for two reasons that run into the analysis. The first is equity. Children are the poorest age group in Argentina: in the second half of 2025, 41.3% of people aged 0 to 14 lived in households below the poverty line, against 9.7% of those aged 65 and over [@indec2026]. Federal resolutions justify the longer day as an instrument for the "sectors of greatest social vulnerability" [@cfe470_2024], while coverage is highest among pupils in the most advantaged socioeconomic category (20.8%), lowest in the middle one (11.8%), and intermediate among the most disadvantaged (17.4%) [@veleda2022]. Whether additional time helps or hurts the most disadvantaged — the distributional question of @sec-lit-latam — is a live feature of the Argentine case and not only a question in the literature.

The second is measurement. The day is lengthened in two ways — some jurisdictions double it, others add a single hour [@veleda2022] — but both became federal policy in 2022 under one programme, 1h+ (@tbl-framework), reported to reach more than eleven thousand schools across twenty-two jurisdictions [@nistal2024; @unahoramas]. The census records both under the same label, so any credible estimate must first separate genuine extension from this administrative expansion (@sec-data-treat, @sec-results-rollout)

```{r}
#| label: fig-provincial-timing
#| fig-cap: "Provincial adoption of the extended day, 2011--2025."
#| out-width: "100%"
exhibit_fig("03_provincial_timing.png")
```

```{=latex}
\fignote{Shading is the share of a province's primary schools whose expanded
enrolment reaches the 50\% treatment threshold in that year, on the annual
census. The unit here is the \emph{province}, which is where adoption is
decided; the estimator itself runs at the level of the \emph{school}
(\S5.2), so a pale row is a jurisdiction in which few schools crossed the
threshold and not one in which the policy was absent. Adoption is staggered
across jurisdictions and reverses in places: Santa Cruz goes from 6.8\% in
2021 to 82.2\% in 2022 and 83.1\% in 2023, then falls to 22.7\% in 2024 and
18.5\% in 2025, the provincial council having suspended the programme for the
2024 school year. That reversal is the non-absorbing treatment the estimator is
chosen for. At the other end, Corrientes and San Luis never exceed 5.3\% and
7.3\% in any year of the census.}
```

# Data and measurement {#sec-data}

## Sources and linkage {#sec-data-sources}

This study combines two administrative sources produced by the same national office, the *Subsecretaría de Información y Evaluación Educativa*. The first is the RA, an annual census of every school in the country, here restricted to establishments offering primary education in at least one year between 2011 and 2025. The second is *Aprender*, the national standardised assessment of grade-6 students, in the six waves that measure both mathematics and language: 2016, 2018, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2025, of which 2022 is a school-level sample and the rest censuses. The RA supplies the treatment, structural covariates and a secondary outcome; *Aprender* supplies the achievement outcomes and pupil composition.

The two sources are linked at the school level by a 15-digit fictitious identifier the agency assigns consistently across them, and linkage is near-complete: between `r link_lo`% and `r link_hi`% of assessed schools match a census record in every wave (@tbl-match). The resulting estimation panel comprises `r n_sw` school-waves within the longer annual census, which tracks each school's treatment from 2011 to 2025. It is unbalanced — a school contributes only in the waves it was assessed, and just `r bal_pct`% appear in all six — but the estimators used below are built for unbalanced panels and do not require a school to be observed throughout.

*Aprender* does not reach every school: of the `r n_prim` schools ever recorded as primary across 2011--2025, about `r cov_pct`% are assessed at least once, and `r n_sch` carry both a score and a treatment history — the estimation sample. What it misses is not a random remainder: within census waves, unassessed schools are far smaller (median primary enrolment `r med_out` against `r med_in`) and much less often treated (`r trt_out`% against `r trt_in`%). The estimand is therefore local to schools large enough to be assessed, and the results should not be read as covering the smallest tail of the primary system.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-match
#| tbl-cap: "Linkage of the *Aprender* assessment to the annual school census, by wave."
if (!is.null(.mr)) {
  tab <- data.table(
    Wave     = as.character(.mr$year),
    Frame    = fifelse(.mr$wave_type == "census", "Census", "Sample"),
    Assessed = fmtn(.mr$schools),
    Matched  = fmtn(.mr$matched_ra),
    Rate     = sprintf("%.2f", .mr$match_rate))
  kbl(tab, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"),
      col.names = c("Wave", "Frame", "Assessed", "Matched", "Match rate")) |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position") |>
    add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Schools" = 2, "Per cent" = 1)) |>
    tbl_note(
      "Schools assessed by \\\\emph{Aprender} in grade 6, and those linking to ",
      "an RA census record in the same year, by assessment wave. Linkage is on the ",
      "agency's 15-digit anonymised school identifier.")
} else exhibit_tbl("01_match_rate_by_wave.csv")
```

## Treatment construction {#sec-data-treat}

The RA records neither a school's schedule as a category nor the daily hours it runs; it records only counts of primary pupils by regime — extended (more than 4 hours) or full (8 hours) — since a school may run the longer day for only part of its enrolment. What it does give is the expanded share of primary enrolment under those regimes, which spans grades 1 to 7 (@sec-context). That share is coverage, not intensity in hours; since the theory-relevant dose is hours, which the RA does not record, treatment is a binary indicator on the share rather than a continuous dose, marking schools where it reaches 50% (@eq-treat).[^dose] The indicator is contemporaneous — whether the school clears the threshold in a given year, and nothing else. Persistence is not imposed: on the annual history the longer day is markedly *non-absorbing* (@sec-strategy-est), and requiring the threshold to hold across adjacent years would smooth away the very oscillation the estimator is built to handle.

[^dose]: The share is not a continuous dose: it measures the fraction of pupils under the longer-day regime, not the length of their day, and instructional time (@sec-lit-time) operates on hours, which the census never records. Intensity in that sense is observable only from the directors' reported hours, and enters through the hours-verified estimates of @sec-results-rollout.

A final step separates two schedules the RA records alike. The federal *1h+* programme funds both a genuine extension and a fifth hour bolted onto an otherwise simple four-hour day [@rm1765_2022; @unahoramas], and the census may record the resulting five-hour school as "extended". The directors' questionnaire reports grade-6 daily hours in the 2021, 2022 and 2023 waves (items `dp23`, `dp18`, `dp47`); each school takes a single time-invariant label from the *highest* it ever reports — *genuine* (six or more), *five-hour*, or *simple* (four or fewer) — a fixed label, since classifying hours wave-by-wave would let treatment flicker between five and six, and is kept only as a sensitivity check. The label identifies the schedule a school runs, not the programme it joined, which the data do not record; timing still comes from the census. Where hours are never observed the census label stands, conservative before the programme existed (@sec-results-rollout). @tbl-treatdef lists every construction and the role each plays.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-treatdef
#| tbl-cap: "Every construction of treatment used below."
# Definitional, not estimated: thresholds are design constants like the choice of
# estimator, so they are typed here as in @tbl-threats. The estimates that go with
# each row are in @tbl-rob-treatdef and @tbl-rob-specs.

td <- data.table(
  Construction = c("Share $\\geq$ 50\\% (primary)",
                   "Share $>$ 0, $\\geq$ 40\\%, $\\geq$ 60\\%, $\\geq$ 75\\%",
                   "Full-day arm",
                   "Hours-verified arms",
                   "Grade-6-enrolment weights"),
  Definition = c(
    "$D_{gt}=\\mathbf{1}\\{s_{gt}\\geq 0.5\\}$, evaluated in the year itself",
    "The same indicator at other cut-offs of the expanded share",
    "$\\mathbf{1}\\{$full-day share $\\geq 0.5\\}$, on the full-day count alone",
    "Directors' reported daily hours: six or more, exactly five, four or fewer",
    "The same $D_{gt}$, with schools weighted by grade-6 enrolment"),
  Role = c("Main specification",
           "Robustness --- same estimand",
           "Different treatment: an eight-hour day, against all other regimes",
           "Different treatment: the schedule actually run, not the regime recorded",
           "Re-targets the estimand: the average pupil, not the average school"))
kbl(td, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", escape = FALSE, align = "l") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 8) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "3.2cm") |> column_spec(2, width = "5.6cm") |>
  column_spec(3, width = "5.0cm") |>
  tbl_note(
    "Only the first is the main specification; the last three answer different questions rather than checking the same one. The distinction in the last column is not presentational. The row marked as ",
    "robustness varies a decision that could defensibly have been made otherwise and ",
    "should leave the same parameter where it is; the last three estimate something ",
    "else, so disagreement with the main specification is information about which ",
    "question is being asked rather than evidence of fragility. Weighting in particular ",
    "moves the mathematics estimate, and that is a finding rather than a failure.")
```

## Outcomes {#sec-data-out}

The primary outcomes are school mean scores in mathematics and language on *Aprender*'s item-response scale, anchored to the 2016 reference (mean 500, standard deviation 100) so that scores are comparable across waves. Following the assessment's official methodology, school means are unweighted: the survey weights correct jurisdiction- and sector-level totals, not within-school averages. Effects are reported in standard-deviation units of that fixed scale. Because each wave assesses a fresh grade-6 cohort, the outcome is a repeated cross-section of school performance rather than a value-added measure following the same pupils.

A secondary outcome uses the census directly: annual grade-6 grade progression — non-promotion (repetition) and dropout — available every year, offering a longer pre-treatment window and a check on whether treatment changes the composition of who sits the exam (Appendix C).

## Ethics and data governance {#sec-data-ethics}

This project underwent the LSE research ethics review process prior to any analysis. Because it relies solely on secondary administrative records, already pseudonymised at source, with no contact with the population under study, the review returned that no further approval was required.

The data are nonetheless restricted, not public. They were obtained from the *Subsecretaría de Información y Evaluación Educativa* under a signed confidentiality agreement, in a release where each school carries a fictitious code rather than its real identifier. All analysis is conducted at the school level or above, never at the level of identifiable individuals, and the replication materials contain only code and aggregate outputs, not the underlying microdata.

# Empirical strategy {#sec-strategy}

The research design is a difference-in-differences with staggered adoption: each school's mean score is compared before and after it crosses the treatment threshold with the scores of schools that have not yet crossed it, and the estimates are read as an event study in time since adoption, identified under parallel trends (@sec-strategy-assump). One feature of the setting shapes the estimator below: because provincial funding is switched on and off, a school can cross the threshold, fall back, and cross again, so adoption is staggered but not absorbing.

## The estimand {#sec-strategy-estimand}

The parameter of interest is a school-level intention-to-treat effect. Let $Y_{gt}$ be the mean grade-6 score of school $g$ in wave $t$, $D_{gt}\in\{0,1\}$ the extended- or full-day indicator, and $Y_{gt}(1)$, $Y_{gt}(0)$ the potential outcomes under the two regimes. The target is:

$$
\tau = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\,Y_{gt}(1) - Y_{gt}(0) \mid D_{gt}=1\,\right],
$$ {#eq-estimand}

the average effect on the schools that actually operate the longer day. Two features of @eq-estimand are decisions rather than defaults, and each is stated here: the unit is the school, and the effect is intention-to-treat.

The unit is the school, not the pupil: the policy is adopted by schools, exposure is recorded for schools, and the outcome is a school mean. Weighting by enrolment targets a different quantity, the effect on the pupil the system is more likely to contain; that is a legitimate object rather than a robustness check, and is reported as such in @sec-results-headline.

And $\tau$ is an intention-to-treat effect, comparing schools by the regime they operate rather than by the hours any grade-6 cohort received. Two gaps separate treatment from outcome: the count is for the cycle rather than the grade (@sec-context), and no record links a pupil to the schedule they attend. The first gap is bounded by arithmetic rather than assumed: grade-6 exposure is forced in `r g6b()`% of treated school-years, rising from `r g6b(2016)`% in the first wave to `r g6b(2025)`% in the last. That bounds whether grade 6 is exposed, not what share of it is, and not the individual-level effect: peer effects, resource reallocation and compositional change can move the school- and pupil-level parameters apart in either direction.

The treated set is defined by the expanded share crossing one half. Writing $s_{gt}$ for the share of primary enrolment in an extended or full day,

$$
D_{gt} = \mathbf{1}\{s_{gt} \ge 0.5\}, \qquad
s_{gt} = \frac{N^{\text{ext}}_{gt} + N^{\text{full}}_{gt}}{N_{gt}},
$$ {#eq-treat}

with $N^{\text{ext}}$ and $N^{\text{full}}$ the counts of primary pupils in each regime (@sec-data-treat).

## Estimator choice {#sec-strategy-est}

The estimand is not the estimator. The design is a staggered difference-in-differences, and the primary estimator is therefore that of @dechaisemartindyn2026, which admits treatments that switch more than once and compares switchers with units not yet switched. That choice is forced by the treatment process: the longer day is a provincial programme schools enter and — in the public sector, as provincial transfers are switched on and off (@sec-context) — leave again. `r rev_pct`% of ever-treated schools contract at some point in the annual record, `r readopt_pct`% subsequently re-adopt, and `r n_multi` change regime twice or more, the paths @fig-trajectories illustrates. *Adoption is not absorbing.*

That rules out the estimators built on absorbing adoption. Callaway--Sant'Anna [@callaway2021] identifies group-time effects under a first-treatment cohort structure and is not defined for units that switch back; two-way fixed effects under staggered timing with heterogeneous effects is a weighted average of two-by-two comparisons with possibly negative weights, some using already-treated units as controls [@goodmanbacon2021; @dechaisemartin2020; @sunabraham2021; @baker2026]. Both are reported as comparisons in @sec-robustness — Callaway--Sant'Anna fitted on the subsample that never contracts, two-way fixed effects as a benchmark not expected to identify @eq-estimand.

Writing $F_g$ for the first wave at which $D_{gt}$ changes, the estimator forms at each horizon $\ell$ a double difference: the change in a switcher's score from the wave before its switch, less the same change for schools not yet switched,

$$
\hat\delta_\ell = \mathbb{E}\!\left[Y_{g,F_g-1+\ell} - Y_{g,F_g-1} \mid \text{switcher}\right]
 - \mathbb{E}\!\left[Y_{g,F_g-1+\ell} - Y_{g,F_g-1} \mid \text{not yet switched}\right].
$$ {#eq-did}

The reported effect aggregates the first two horizons, $\hat\delta_1$ and $\hat\delta_2$, weighted by the switchers each supports; later horizons rest on too few switchers to estimate, and are shown but not aggregated (@sec-results-diagnosis). Placebos are the same contrast run backwards over pre-treatment waves.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trajectories
#| fig-cap: "Expanded-day share for illustrative schools, one row per archetype."
#| out-width: "100%"
exhibit_fig("05_school_trajectories.png")
```

```{=latex}
\fignote{The dashed line marks the 50\% treatment threshold (@eq-treat): a
school is treated in the years its share is above it. `One-way exit' and
`oscillator' schools cross the line and fall back, so adoption is not
absorbing --- the property that rules out estimators built on a single,
permanent switch. Schools are drawn from the annual census and are illustrative
of each archetype rather than representative of it; the share is extended- and
full-day enrolment combined, which is the quantity the indicator is defined on.}
```

## Event time: waves, calendar time and exposure {#sec-strategy-time}

Three quantities must be kept apart (@tbl-time): event time, calendar time since the first change, and exposure, the years actually treated. Under an absorbing treatment the last two coincide; here a school can switch on, contract, and be assessed having accumulated fewer treated years than have elapsed. The first coefficient pools calendar distances from the adoption year itself to `r exp_max` years, with `r exp_modal_pct`% at the modal length.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-time
#| tbl-cap: "Event time, calendar time since adoption and exposure: three quantities that come apart under this design and cannot be treated as one."
tq <- data.table(
  Quantity = c("\\textsc{event time}",
               "\\textsc{calendar time since first adoption}",
               "\\textsc{exposure}"),
  Counts = c("Periods since the school's first treatment change",
             "Years between the annual switch and the wave at which the school is assessed",
             "Years the school has actually been treated, $C_{gt}=\\sum_{\\tau=F_g}^{t} D_{g\\tau}$"),
  `Measured in` = c("Assessment waves", "Years", "Years"),
  `Equal to exposure?` = c("Never (waves $\\ne$ years)",
                           "Only under an absorbing treatment",
                           "By definition"))
kbl(tq, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", escape = FALSE, align = "l") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 8) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "3.3cm") |> column_spec(2, width = "6.0cm") |>
  column_spec(3, width = "2.0cm") |> column_spec(4, width = "2.9cm") |>
  tbl_note(
    "The estimator indexes its effects by the first row. The paths $0,1,0,0$ and ",
    "$0,1,1,1$ share an event time and a calendar time and differ in exposure, which is ",
    "why the three cannot be treated as one. The outcome is observed in six waves ",
    "spaced unevenly while treatment is recorded annually, so schools at the same ",
    "event-time index sit at different calendar distances from their own switch.")
```

This matters for the question and not only for the arithmetic. If instructional time is an input with diminishing returns (@sec-lit-time), the theory predicts that the effect should *grow with exposure*. A coefficient averaging a school measured in its adoption year with one measured four years in cannot test that prediction: its weights over calendar distances are a property of the assessment calendar rather than of the policy.

The remedy for outcomes observed less often than the treatment is to partition switchers by where the first change falls relative to the outcome dates and estimate once per partition, using the annual treatment information *only* to select the subsamples [@dechaisemartincompanion2025]. The *Aprender* calendar is irregular rather than periodic, so the partition here is by *calendar time since first adoption*, fixed at every horizon once the wave and the year of the first change are known. Each class is estimated against all never-switching school-waves and classes are not pooled; those holding `r exp_top3_pct`% of switchers are estimated, the remainder reported and not estimated.

One limit is declared rather than absorbed: the partition homogenises calendar time, not exposure — at the second horizon of the one-year class only `r gap_h2_e1`% of schools were treated throughout the elapsed window. Partitioning on years treated would mean leaving the estimator's own event time, anchored at the first change.

## Identifying assumptions {#sec-strategy-assump}

Identification rests on three assumptions. \textsc{Parallel trends}: absent a change in regime, treated and not-yet-treated schools would have followed the same path in mean achievement, conditional on the covariates entering each specification. \textsc{No anticipation}: outcomes before a school's first change do not respond to the change to come — plausible here, since the assessment measures pupils already enrolled and provincial funding decisions are not announced a year ahead. \textsc{SUTVA}: No interference is plausible given dispersed schools and own-pupil outcomes, though shared provincial funding is a channel the not-yet-treated comparison does not close (@sec-strategy-inf). Consistency fails as the census records treatment, bundling five-, six- and eight-hour days; separating them by reported hours is the response (@sec-results-rollout), so the measurement correction is in part a consistency analysis.

The comparison group is *not-yet-treated* rather than never-treated. Never-treated schools here are systematically different — smaller, more rural, more often outside the assessment frame altogether (@sec-data-sources) — so restricting the comparison to them would trade a weaker assumption for a worse-matched counterfactual. The not-yet-treated group keeps the comparison inside the population that eventually adopts, at the cost of requiring that the timing of adoption be unrelated to the counterfactual path — a requirement about when a province contracts and about which schools it then picks within its quota (@sec-context), neither of which is observed.

Baseline covariates enter only the doubly-robust specification: the primary estimator differences within school, so a time-invariant covariate has $\Delta X = 0$ and drops out — time-invariant confounders, observed and unobserved, difference out with it, so identification turns on parallel trends rather than on controlling for them, and differential time-varying confounding is what the placebos probe (@sec-results-diagnosis). That is a property of the estimator, not a judgement about which confounders matter, and it is why the socioeconomic covariate — the characteristic provincial programmes use to select schools (@sec-context) — appears only there. Appendix A sets out which schools that specification drops and how its cohorts are dated.

## Inference {#sec-strategy-inf}

Inference in this design cannot be made to look clean. Two things must be kept apart: the *level* at which dependence is allowed, and the *procedure* that estimates it.

The level is a substantive question, and the design answers it: the province. Adoption is coordinated there, the funding decisions that reverse it are taken there, measurement error in the treatment is structured by jurisdiction (@sec-results-rollout), and untreated shocks may themselves be provincial [@abadie2023]. The estimator's default variance is computed at the group level — here the school — and is reported throughout for comparability, not because the design argues for it.

The procedure admits no clean answer. There are `r n_prov` jurisdictions but they are very unequal, with an effective number near `r eff_sw` [@carter2017], and both available procedures need more independent information across clusters than that supplies. The wild cluster bootstrap [@cameron2008; @mackinnon2018] is defined on regression residuals, so it reaches the two-way fixed-effects benchmark and not the primary estimator; what that estimator offers is a nonparametric pairs cluster bootstrap over whole provinces. Both are reported in @sec-rob-sensitivity and no conclusion turns on either.

Two consequences follow for how the results are read. Because no province-level procedure is reliable at this cluster count, the discussion turns on the size of estimates and their placebos rather than on which side of a threshold a p-value falls (@sec-results-verdict). And because adoption is provincially concentrated, a leverage check is more informative than further intervals: dropping one province at a time moves the wave-indexed mathematics estimate between `r lopo_lo` and `r lopo_hi`, and none takes it across zero — point estimates, not an inference procedure.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-threats
#| tbl-cap: "Threats to identification, the check that addresses each, and what kind of check it is."
threats <- data.table(
  Threat = c("Event time mixes exposure lengths", "Treatment definition drives the result",
             "Grade-6 exposure (whole-primary count)",
             "Score-scale comparability", "Five-hour contamination",
             "Repeated cross-sections change composition",
             "School- vs pupil-average estimand", "Comparison group",
             "Parallel trends (primary estimand)",
             "Parallel trends (absorbing subsample)", "Estimator choice",
             "Within-province dependence in the errors",
             "One adoption cohort drives the disagreement"),
  Check = c("Partition by time since first adoption, estimated separately",
            "Cut-offs 0/40/50/60/75\\%",
            "Pigeonhole bound; grade-6-certain restriction",
            "Within-wave standardisation", "Genuine 6h+ vs five-hour split (directors' hours)",
            "Grade-progression (flow) outcomes",
            "Enrolment-weighted re-estimation", "Never-treated instead of not-yet-treated",
            "Effect against the placebo of the same specification",
            "HonestDiD bounds; equivalence tests", "CDH / CS / FEct / TWFE compared",
            "Province-clustered analytic and resampled SEs; leave-one-province-out points",
            "2023-cohort exclusion; identifying-variation count"),
  # Position 6 is the grade-progression check. It is NOT another way of estimating
  # the achievement effect -- it uses a different outcome to rule out a different
  # threat, that the measured mean moved because a different kind of pupil sat the
  # test -- so it is a composition check and not an alternative implementation.
  Kind = c("Identification", "Robustness", "Robustness", "Robustness", "Robustness",
           "Diagnostic", "Robustness", "Robustness", "Sensitivity",
           "Sensitivity", "Robustness", "Sensitivity", "Diagnostic"))
kbl(threats, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 10) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "4.6cm") |> column_spec(2, width = "6.6cm") |>
  column_spec(3, width = "2.2cm") |>
  tbl_note(paste0(
    "The two parallel-trends rows address different estimands and are not ",
    "interchangeable: the effect-against-placebo comparison is a diagnostic on the ",
    "primary estimand, while the Rambachan--Roth bounds are computed on the ",
    "doubly-robust estimator's absorbing subsample and speak only to it. Resampling ",
    "schemes also differ by estimator -- the wild cluster bootstrap is defined only ",
    "where the estimand is a regression coefficient -- so p-values are not comparable ",
    "across estimators as measures of evidential strength."))
```

# Results {#sec-results}

## What the treatment is {#sec-results-rollout}

Adoption is staggered, and the cohorts are very unequal. @tbl-cohorts dates each school by the year it first crosses the threshold. Most cohorts hold a few hundred schools; two do not. `r coh("already treated in 2011 (left-censored)")` schools already run the longer day in 2011 and are left-censored, with no pre-treatment period. And 2023 holds `r coh("2023")` schools, `r coh("2023", "in_estimation_sample")` in the estimation sample — an order of magnitude above its neighbours. That one cohort supplies most of the identifying variation, and @sec-results-diagnosis returns to it.

The aggregate share of schools running a longer day hides the movement underneath it (@fig-transitions): entries and exits are both large, and the 2023 entry spike is followed at once by contractions in 2024. Over the full annual census, `r rev_pct`% of ever-treated schools later contract. Between assessment waves the movement is smaller — `r tt("increase")`% of transitions are increases, `r tt("decrease")`% decreases (@tbl-switching) — but the annual figure is the one that describes the treatment, since a school that contracts and re-adopts between two waves never shows up in the wave-to-wave count. Adoption is therefore not the absorbing transition the regional evaluations assume, which is why the estimator admits treatment that switches in both directions (@sec-strategy-est).

One feature of the assessment frame runs through everything below. *Aprender* does not reach the smallest schools (@sec-data-sources), so the same size-dependent coverage decides which schools contribute to each horizon. Adopting and never-adopting schools differ on structure, not on baseline achievement (@tbl-balance) — a difference that matters as the burden the conditional parallel-trends assumption carries, not as imbalance in levels, which differencing removes.

The census records a five-hour day under the same label as a genuine six- or eight-hour one (@sec-data-treat); the directors' reported hours tell them apart. @fig-contamination puts the split where it matters. Of the `r ctm_n("adopted <2023 (stock)")` schools recorded as extended in 2023 that had adopted earlier — the stock — `r ctm("adopted <2023 (stock)", "genuine")`% report 6 hours or more; of the `r ctm_n("adopted 2023 (flow)")` adopting in 2023 — the flow — only `r ctm("adopted 2023 (flow)", "genuine")`% do, and `r ctm("adopted 2023 (flow)", "horamas")`% report exactly five. The stock is almost all genuine; the flow is majority five-hour; and the flow is what identifies the effect, because a staggered design is built on the schools that switch.

The problem is the variable, not one year. The census records a *category* each jurisdiction defines for itself (@sec-context); the questionnaire asks a *quantity* that means the same everywhere, so one can be used to audit the other. The census's recording rate rises with reported hours — in 2023, `r rec23("4h or less")`% at 4 hours or less, `r rec23("5h")`% at five, `r rec23("6h")`% at six, `r rec23("7h or more")`% at seven or more — tracking the length of the day everywhere except at the five-hour step. The yardstick is thin (at most three reports per school, and 2022 only for sampled schools), so it is stated here rather than relied on silently. But the failure is not new: in 2021, before the federal programme, the five-hour rate was already `r rec(2021, "5h")`% against `r rec(2021, "6h or more")`% at 6 hours or more. The instrument did not deteriorate; the population moved — schools reporting exactly five hours rose from `r nrec(2021, "5h")` to `r nrec(2023, "5h")`, tripling the number standing exactly where the variable fails.

The error runs both ways, and only one way is merely descriptive. Where a five-hour school is recorded as extended, the aggregate overstates genuine extension: `r fhm("% of census extended day that is a five-hour school")`% of what the census calls extended day in 2023 is a five-hour school. Where it is not recorded, the aggregate understates it, and `r fhm("of which left in the comparison group")` five-hour schools stay in the comparison group. The second is a threat to identification, not just to description: part of the untreated group has in fact received a smaller dose of the same intervention, and the misclassification is neither classical nor independent of jurisdiction.

The jurisdictional pattern is not a provincial reporting rule — schools, not provinces, complete the census. It is that the federal programme took a different name, schedule and legal form in each jurisdiction (@tbl-provincias), on top of provincial models that already differed [@veleda2013], so a school reports in its own jurisdiction's category. That this is framing, not noise, shows where the object is unambiguous: in 2021, of the `r p21_n` jurisdictions with at least thirty schools reporting 6 hours or more, all but one record them at between `r p21_lo`% and `r p21_hi`% — the exception being `r if (!is.null(p21_out)) p21_out$province else "[n/a]"`, where the simple day legally runs to 25 weekly hours. The closest Argentine antecedent reached the same judgement from the other side, restricting its use of this variable to years up to 2019 [@veleda2022].

Separating the two schedules leaves the average almost unchanged, as contamination in the flow rather than the stock implies: `r arm("genuine 6h+ (stable)", "mathematics")` in mathematics on schools verified at 6 hours or more, `r arm("1h+ 5h (stable)", "mathematics")` on the five-hour schools, neither distinguishable from zero (@tbl-arms). Whatever positive estimate exists belongs to genuine extension; the five-hour day alone cannot be shown to move test scores. The correction is therefore not a rescue of the estimates but a finding about the statistics used to report progress on the legal commitment — statistics that do not measure what the commitment is about.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-arms

# The combined arm is the headline specification of 06; the two separated arms
# come from 08. They are shown together because the point of the table is that
```
