```{r}
if (!is.null(.arm) && !is.null(.m)) {
  gA <- function(e, s, cv = "none (absorbed)")
    .m[estimator == e & regime == "combined" & subject == s & covariates == cv]
  gR <- function(e, a, s) .arm[estimator == e & arm == a & subject == s]
  arms <- c("genuine 6h+ (stable)", "1h+ 5h (stable)")
  labs <- c("Combined (all recorded extension)", "Genuine 6h+ extension",
            "Five-hour day")
  val <- function(e, s, col) c(
    if (e == "CDH") gA("CDH (headline)", s)[[col]] else gA("CS (absorbing)", s, "none")[[col]],
    vapply(arms, function(a) { v <- gR(e, a, s)[[col]]
      if (length(v) == 0) NA_real_ else v }, numeric(1)))
  # Three stacked lines per cell: estimate, standard error, N. N cannot be one
  # column of the table because it differs by estimator as well as by arm -- the
  # doubly-robust rows run on the absorbing subsample with complete covariates
  # and so rest on far fewer school-waves than the primary estimator does.
  cell <- function(e, s) { est <- val(e, s, "att"); se <- val(e, s, "se")
    n <- val(e, s, "n_obs")
    as.vector(rbind(ifelse(is.na(est), "--", sprintf("%.3f", est)),
                    ifelse(is.na(se),  "",   sprintf("(%.3f)", se)),
                    ifelse(is.na(n),   "",   fmtn(n)))) }
  tab <- data.table(Arm = as.vector(rbind(labs, "", "")),
                    a = cell("CDH", "language"), b = cell("CDH", "mathematics"),
                    c = cell("CS",  "language"), d = cell("CS",  "mathematics"))
  kbl(tab, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
      col.names = c("Verified schedule", "(1)", "(2)", "(3)", "(4)")) |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position") |>
    add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Language" = 1, "Mathematics" = 1,
                       "Language" = 1, "Mathematics" = 1)) |>
    add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Primary estimator (CDH)" = 2,
                       "Doubly robust (CS)" = 2)) |>
    tbl_note(
      "The arms separate what the census records as extension into genuine six-hour extension and the five-hour day recorded alongside it. Standard errors in parentheses. Outcome in standard-deviation units of the ",
      "2016 anchored scale. Treatment is the main binary indicator ",
      "(expanded share $\\\\geq$ 50\\\\% in the year), comparison group not-yet-treated, ",
      "aggregating the first two post-treatment horizons; variance is the ",
      "estimator's analytical group-level variance, the group being the school. ",
      "Province-level and resampled uncertainty for this specification are in ",
      "the appendix; the two procedures disagree materially and neither is treated ",
      "as authoritative (\\S7.2). ",
      "Arms are assigned from the directors' reported grade-6 daily hours, taken ",
      "at the highest a school ever reports, so the label is time-invariant while ",
      "the timing of treatment still comes from the census. That rule is ",
      "consequential and not one-directional: taking the peak lifts a school into ",
      "the five-hour class from below and out of it from above at once, so ",
      lr("five-hour under the peak rule"), " schools are classed five-hour under it ",
      "against ", lr("five-hour under the modal rule"), " under a modal rule and ",
      lr("five-hour under the last-reported rule"), " under a last-reported one. ",
      "The contamination shares reported in the text are computed from each wave's ",
      "own reported hours and are not exposed to this choice. The five-hour arm ",
      "is compared against untreated schools with no five-hour schools among them. ",
      "Callaway--Sant'Anna requires absorbing adoption and is fitted on the ",
      "non-contracting subsample, so columns (3) and (4) rest on a different ",
      "population. It is not estimated for the five-hour arm because three ",
      "quarters of that arm adopts in a single wave, leaving its other cohorts ",
      "too small for the doubly-robust regression each cohort-period cell ",
      "requires: the dash is a limit of the estimator, not a zero.")
} else exhibit_tbl("08_arm_results.csv")
```

## The effect on achievement {#sec-results-headline}

Estimated on the full panel and indexed by assessment wave, the primary estimator returns `r hz(2, "language")` in language and `r hz(2, "mathematics")` in mathematics, in standard-deviation units of the anchored 2016 scale, aggregating the two post-treatment horizons the design supports (Panel A of @tbl-main). Both are small against the regional benchmark of about 0.04 standard deviations at primary level [@alvarez2019], and only the mathematics estimate reaches conventional significance. It does so, however, only in that aggregation window: one horizon gives `r hz(1, "mathematics")` (*t* `r hz(1, "mathematics", col = "t")`) and three give `r hz(3, "mathematics")` (*t* `r hz(3, "mathematics", col = "t")`), because the entire positive sits in the second horizon, which is supported by `r hz_n(2)` switching schools against `r hz_n(1)` at the first.

The window is reported alongside the estimate rather than resolved by choosing one, since moving it after seeing where significance lies would be specification search in reverse. A deeper issue: the index is in waves, and waves are not exposure (@sec-strategy-time). Classifying switchers by the calendar time between their first adoption and the wave at which they are assessed, and estimating each class separately against all never-switching schools, mathematics gives `r pj(0, "mathematics")` for schools assessed in their adoption year, `r pj(1, "mathematics")` at one year and `r pj(2, "mathematics")` at two. No cumulative pattern appears. What the partition establishes is narrower than a dose-response claim: the classes are not the same schools observed at different durations but different schools, differing also in adoption cohort, calendar and composition. The pattern survives the window in which calendar time is fully homogeneous, where the classes give `r pj(0, "mathematics", sp = "1 horizon")`, `r pj(1, "mathematics", sp = "1 horizon")` and `r pj(2, "mathematics", sp = "1 horizon")`.

The class that carries the positive is also the class in which it can least be separated from what preceded it. Its estimated effect is `r pj(0, "mathematics")` and its own pre-treatment placebo is `r pj(0, "mathematics", par = "Placebo_1")` — the same magnitude, on the same schools, before treatment (@tbl-timing-placebo). It is, in addition, the class in which the 2023 adoption cohort is concentrated, while the one-year class contains none of it. Several independent diagnostics therefore locate the fragility in the same cohort and the same window, which is what the data support and is weaker than a claim that the positive estimate and the pre-treatment difference are one phenomenon.

The pooled placebo conceals this rather than contradicting it, and only if one placebo is read where the specification reports two. The first is near zero in both subjects, `r mp("mathematics")` in mathematics and `r mp("language")` in language. The second is `r mp("mathematics", "Placebo_2")` in mathematics (s.e. `r mp("mathematics", "Placebo_2", "se")`), the same estimate as the *k* = −2 lead of @fig-eventstudy: placebos and event-study leads are one diagnostic reported twice, not two that agree. By class the placebos are `r pj(0, "mathematics", par = "Placebo_1")`, `r pj(1, "mathematics", par = "Placebo_1")` and `r pj(2, "mathematics", par = "Placebo_1")`, and their switcher-weighted mean reproduces the pooled value: the class point estimates offset one another. A near-zero pooled placebo therefore averages class estimates of opposite sign rather than showing small pre-treatment differences — cancellation among point estimates, not demonstrated parallel trends.

Three limits qualify it. Partitioning costs precision: the class standard errors are `r pj(1, "mathematics", col = "se")` and `r pj(2, "mathematics", col = "se")` against `r hz(2, "mathematics", col = "se")` pooled, and no class individually excludes the pooled estimate. The classes homogenise calendar time and not years treated (@sec-strategy-time). And none is promoted in place of the pooled coefficient, since choosing after seeing which produces the positive would be an *ex post* choice. What changes is the coefficient's status rather than its value: it is reported with the partition beside it and is not the study's primary result, because an average over materially different distances from adoption cannot be translated back onto a single calendar.

Panel A's third quantity answers a different question rather than checking this one. Weighting by grade-6 enrolment targets the average effect on the pupil rather than on the school — the estimand policy is framed in — and takes mathematics from `r mn("CDH (headline)", "mathematics")` to `r mn("CDH (grade-6-weighted)", "mathematics")`, the two estimator families agreeing once weighted (@tbl-main). A per-school effect does not carry over proportionally to the per-pupil parameter, and that is not evidence of larger effects in small schools: weighting re-weights size, rurality, composition, province and adoption cohort at once.

Fixing the set of switchers across horizons moves it the other way — mathematics rises to `r opt("2 horizons, same switchers", "mathematics")` — but is not promoted either: that population is selected by its capacity to sustain a second horizon, and its placebo rises in step.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-main
#| tbl-cap: "Effect of extended-day operation on grade-6 achievement."
# Panel A: the pooled specification, the same estimand partitioned by time since
# first adoption, and the pupil-average re-weighting. Panel B: four estimators on
# the common sample of 11b. Standard errors in parentheses. The three tables are
# read in the setup chunk, because the prose quotes them before the table runs.

# Estimate over its standard error, as two stacked rows, in the applied-micro
# convention. `key` names the row block so the panels can be assembled by label.
coef_block <- function(labels, est, se, extra = NULL) {
  out <- data.table(Specification = as.vector(rbind(labels, "")),
                    Language      = as.vector(rbind(sprintf("%.3f", est$lang),
                                                    sprintf("(%.3f)", se$lang))),
                    Mathematics   = as.vector(rbind(sprintf("%.3f", est$math),
                                                    sprintf("(%.3f)", se$math))))
  if (!is.null(extra)) out <- cbind(out[, 1], extra, out[, 2:3])
  out
}

pick <- function(dt, ...) { r <- dt[...]; setNames(r$att, r$subject) }

if (!is.null(.m) && !is.null(.pj) && !is.null(.lf)) {
  gA <- function(e, s) .m[estimator == e & regime == "combined" & subject == s]
  gJ <- function(x, s, p) .pj[definition == "main" & spec == PJ_WINDOW &
                              exposure_years == x & subject == s & parameter == p]

  labsA <- c("Pooled, two horizons",
             "  Adoption year", "  One year", "  Two years",
             "Pupil-weighted (grade-6 enrolment)")
  estA <- list(
    lang = c(gA("CDH (headline)", "language")$att,
             sapply(0:2, function(x) gJ(x, "language", "ATE")$estimate),
             gA("CDH (grade-6-weighted)", "language")$att),
    math = c(gA("CDH (headline)", "mathematics")$att,
             sapply(0:2, function(x) gJ(x, "mathematics", "ATE")$estimate),
             gA("CDH (grade-6-weighted)", "mathematics")$att))
  seA <- list(
    lang = c(gA("CDH (headline)", "language")$se,
             sapply(0:2, function(x) gJ(x, "language", "ATE")$se),
             gA("CDH (grade-6-weighted)", "language")$se),
    math = c(gA("CDH (headline)", "mathematics")$se,
             sapply(0:2, function(x) gJ(x, "mathematics", "ATE")$se),
             gA("CDH (grade-6-weighted)", "mathematics")$se))
  A <- coef_block(labsA, estA, seA)

  ord <- c("CDH (did_multiplegt_dyn)", "Callaway-Sant'Anna",
           "FEct (FE imputation)", "FEct (interactive FE)", "TWFE")
  gL <- function(e, s) .lf[estimator == e & subject == s]
  B <- coef_block(ord,
    list(lang = sapply(ord, function(e) gL(e, "language")$att),
         math = sapply(ord, function(e) gL(e, "mathematics")$att)),
    list(lang = sapply(ord, function(e) gL(e, "language")$se),
         math = sapply(ord, function(e) gL(e, "mathematics")$se)),
    extra = data.table(`Counterfactual trend` =
      as.vector(rbind(sapply(ord, function(e) gL(e, "language")$counterfactual_trend), ""))))
  A[, `Counterfactual trend` := ""]
  setcolorder(A, names(B))

  tab <- rbind(A, B)
  kbl(tab, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = c("l", "l", "r", "r"),
      col.names = c("Specification", "Counterfactual trend", "Language", "Mathematics")) |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position")) |>
    pack_rows("Panel A. Primary estimator", 1, nrow(A)) |>
    pack_rows("Panel B. Estimator comparison, common sample", nrow(A) + 1, nrow(tab)) |>
    tbl_note(paste0(
      "Standard errors in parentheses. Estimator: de Chaisemartin--D'Haultf\\\\oe uille ",
      "\\\\texttt{did\\\\_multiplegt\\\\_dyn} unless stated. Variance is the estimator's ",
      "analytical group-level variance; the group is the school. Panel A aggregates ",
      "the first two post-treatment horizons on the full estimation sample of ",
      n_sch, " schools and ", n_sw, " school-waves; its indented rows partition ",
      "switchers by time since first adoption and estimate each class separately ",
      "against all never-switching schools, so they are not pooled with one another. ",
      "Panel B aggregates three horizons on the non-reverting subsample, the window ",
      "and sample that make the estimators comparable at matched event times; that ",
      "difference in window, not a conflict, is why its first row differs from the ",
      "pooled row above. Panel B rows are not estimates of a common parameter on an ",
      "identical population -- Callaway--Sant'Anna requires absorbing adoption, and ",
      "the estimators differ in the counterfactual trend they assume -- so agreement ",
      "or disagreement between them is suggestive rather than a specification test."))
} else {
  kbl(data.frame(Status = "exhibit pending: 06_estimation_main.csv / 06j / 11b"),
      booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-timing-placebo
#| tbl-cap: "Post-treatment effect and the corresponding pre-treatment placebo, by time since first adoption."
# The identification argument in one exhibit: wherever a positive effect appears,
# the placebo of the same specification is of comparable size. Effects repeat the
# indented rows of Panel A of @tbl-main; they are shown again because the pairing,
# not either column alone, is what the table is for.
if (!is.null(.pj)) {
  g <- function(x, s, p) .pj[definition == "main" & spec == PJ_WINDOW &
                             exposure_years == x & subject == s & parameter == p]
  labs <- c("Adoption year", "One year", "Two years")
  cell <- function(s, p) as.vector(rbind(
    sapply(0:2, function(x) sprintf("%.3f", g(x, s, p)$estimate)),
    sapply(0:2, function(x) sprintf("(%.3f)", g(x, s, p)$se))))
  tab <- data.table(
    `Time since first adoption` = as.vector(rbind(labs, "")),
    `Effect`  = cell("language", "ATE"),      `Placebo` = cell("language", "Placebo_1"),
    `Effect ` = cell("mathematics", "ATE"),   `Placebo ` = cell("mathematics", "Placebo_1"))
  kbl(tab, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
      col.names = c("Time since first adoption", "Effect", "Placebo", "Effect", "Placebo")) |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position")) |>
    add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Language" = 2, "Mathematics" = 2)) |>
    tbl_note(paste0(
      "Standard errors in parentheses. Each class is estimated separately against all ",
      "never-switching schools and aggregates the first two post-treatment horizons; ",
      "classes are not pooled with one another. The placebo is the estimator's own ",
      "pre-treatment coefficient for the same specification. Classes are defined by ",
      "time since the first adoption, which in a non-absorbing design is not the same ",
      "as years actually treated; see the discussion of event time in the empirical ",
      "strategy. Under the pooled specification ",
      "the placebo is small in both subjects; that value is the switcher-weighted mean ",
      "of the three shown here, whose signs differ."))
} else {
  kbl(data.frame(Status = "exhibit pending: 06j_exposure_partition.csv"),
      booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "")
}
```

## What the diagnostics show, and why the estimators disagree {#sec-results-diagnosis}

What follows is evidence on observed pre-treatment differences, not on the assumption itself: parallel trends concerns a counterfactual path that is never observed, so a placebo that fails to reject does not establish it, and one that rejects establishes only prior divergence. Three problems are kept apart: the population identifying each horizon changes (@sec-results-headline); a significant placebo is direct evidence of differential trends; and the tests have limited power, so a small placebo with a wide interval does not separate absence from imprecision — a caution the estimator's own authors repeat about these placebos, which may fail to detect violations large enough to bias the estimates [@roth2022; @dechaisemartindyn2026].

The event study of the primary estimator (@fig-eventstudy) carries the direct evidence. In mathematics the second lead is `r es(-2, "Mathematics")`, excluding zero under the estimator's default variance and of the same order as any effect estimated in this study, while the lead immediately before adoption is `r es(-1, "Mathematics")` and does not reject; language gives `r es(-2, "Language")` and `r es(-1, "Language")`, neither distinguishable from zero.

Two explanations for that lead can be ruled out. It is not composition: contemporaneous controls leave it at `r esx(-2, "Mathematics", "composition-controlled")` and baseline covariates in the doubly-robust estimator at `r esc(-2, "Mathematics", sp = "baseline-covariates")`. Nor is it the score scale, a reasonable suspicion given the documented uncertainty about the 2021 equating (@sec-data-out): standardising within wave, which is immune to scale drift, takes the same placebo from `r sc("Mathematics", "anchored /100")` to `r sc("Mathematics", "within-wave z")`. What remains is identification.

```{r}
#| label: fig-eventstudy
#| fig-cap: "Event-study estimates from the primary estimator."
exhibit_fig("07_event_study_cdh.png")
```

```{=latex}
\fignote{Points are the ATT at each event time in assessment waves, with 95\% confidence bands; the number of switching schools identifying each post-treatment horizon is printed under its tick, and it collapses as the horizon grows. Mathematics shows one placebo excluding zero, at the second lead, of the same order as any effect estimated in this study; language shows none at either lead. Leads are evidence on observed pre-treatment differences, not on parallel trends, which concerns a counterfactual path that is never observed.}
```

A second symptom points the same way. The sign of the effect is not robust to the model assumed for the counterfactual trend: on the common sample of Panel B of @tbl-main the primary estimator gives `r lf("CDH (did_multiplegt_dyn)", "mathematics")` in mathematics and the doubly-robust one `r lf("Callaway-Sant'Anna", "mathematics")`, both positive, while the imputation estimator [@liu2024] gives `r lf("FEct (FE imputation)", "mathematics")` and two-way fixed effects `r lf("TWFE", "mathematics")`, both negative and, with dependence allowed only within school, both distinguishable from zero — a precision that province-level resampling substantially weakens (@sec-rob-sensitivity).

Carryover and reversal are ruled out as explanations: both leave the disagreement in place (@tbl-app-carryover).

What remains is the counterfactual trend each family imposes, the column Panel B reports. The primary and doubly-robust estimators build local comparisons against not-yet-treated schools; the imputation and fixed-effects estimators impose one common set of time effects on every school. Where treated and comparison schools follow different paths, that restriction is false, and the estimators relying on it record the difference as a negative effect.

The two symptoms have one source, and it is narrower than the design as a whole. By adoption cohort (@tbl-decomp) the pre-treatment placebo is `r cd(2023)` for the 2023 cohort and small and insignificant for every other, and that cohort's last untreated observation is the 2021 post-pandemic wave. Excluding the cohort resolves several apparently separate symptoms at once: the imputation estimator's joint pre-treatment test stops rejecting in both subjects, in mathematics from *p* = `r sg("full", "mathematics", "pretrend_f_p")` to `r sg("excl. 2023 cohort", "mathematics", "pretrend_f_p")`; its estimates move to `r sg("excl. 2023 cohort", "language")` and `r sg("excl. 2023 cohort", "mathematics")`, neither distinguishable from zero; the mathematics second lead falls to `r cvr("exclude 2023 cohort (full waves)", "math_k2")`, no longer significant; and in language the three families agree. The mechanism is not established — the pandemic, changes in the assessment, uneven recovery and the federal programme are all consistent with it. What is established is that the concern is localised to one comparison rather than being a uniform divergence.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-decomp
#| tbl-cap: "The mathematics pre-treatment placebo by adoption cohort."
# Only the k = -2 row of the group-time decomposition, and only mathematics: the
# table exists to locate one placebo, not to reproduce the event study.
.cd <- read_out("07b_cohort_decomposition.csv")
if (!is.null(.cd)) {
  z <- .cd[k == -2 & subject == "mathematics"][order(g_year)]
  tab <- data.table(`Adoption cohort` = as.vector(rbind(as.character(z$g_year), "")),
                    Comparison = as.vector(rbind(sprintf("%d to %d", z$t_year, z$g_year), "")),
                    Placebo    = as.vector(rbind(sprintf("%.3f", z$att),
                                                 sprintf("(%.3f)", z$se))))
  kbl(tab, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = c("l", "l", "r")) |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position")) |>
    tbl_note(paste0(
      "Each row is a group-time estimate two periods before adoption, so the comparison years that produce it are named alongside it: the cohort carrying the placebo is the one whose last untreated comparison spans the 2021 post-pandemic wave. Standard errors in parentheses. Callaway--Sant'Anna group-time estimates on the ",
      "absorbing subsample, mathematics, at the second pre-treatment period. Cohorts are ",
      "dated by the first wave at which a school is observed treated, so the comparison ",
      "column gives the two assessment years the estimate differences. The 2022 cohort is ",
      "small because only schools drawn into the 2022 sample wave can belong to it."))
} else {
  kbl(data.frame(Status = "exhibit pending: 07b_cohort_decomposition.csv"),
      booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "")
}
```

In mathematics the families do not converge. The doubly-robust estimator stays at `r cvr("exclude 2023 cohort (full waves)", "cs_math")` while the other two sit near zero, so the cohort accounts for the pre-treatment symptoms and for the language disagreement but not for the residual dispersion in mathematics. That dispersion has a separate and measured explanation: the doubly-robust estimator runs on the absorbing subsample, which discards the schools that contract, and those are systematically larger, so its population is tilted towards smaller schools. Weighting by enrolment closes the gap (@sec-results-headline), which is what a difference driven by the composition of the sample rather than by the counterfactual trend should do.

Language is not the clean case by contrast: on the absorbing subsample the doubly-robust estimator excludes zero at its two most distant leads. Mathematics shows a differential trend close to adoption and localised to one cohort, language one only at distant leads and under another estimator; neither pre-treatment trajectory can be called parallel.

The full-day estimate, which would otherwise look strongest — mathematics `r hz(2, "mathematics", rg = "full-day")`, stable across windows — is rejected by its own first placebo, significant and larger than the effect it precedes, and so is not read causally; in language the full-day placebo is null. How large a violation would overturn the remaining estimates is taken up in @sec-rob-sensitivity, where bounds [@rambachan2023] exist only for the doubly-robust estimator.

Two limits qualify the diagnostic. Excluding the cohort changes the estimand: it removes the largest single source of identifying variation, `r 100 - as.numeric(ivr("observed_0to1"))`% of all observed adoptions, so it is a probe and no estimate is reported on that sample as a primary estimate. And the convergence is not merely the loss of variation that would make any two estimators agree: the exclusion retains `r ivr("schools")`% of schools and `r hz_ret(1)`% and `r hz_ret(2)`% of the switchers supporting the first two horizons (@tbl-app-idvar).

## What the estimates support {#sec-results-verdict}

One pattern orders the chapter. Wherever a positive estimate of relevant magnitude appears, the placebo of the same specification reports a pre-treatment difference at least as large: `r hz(2, "mathematics")` against `r mp("mathematics", "Placebo_2")` in the pooled specification itself, `r pj(0, "mathematics")` against `r pj(0, "mathematics", par = "Placebo_1")` in the class assessed in the adoption year, `r opt("2 horizons, same switchers", "mathematics")` against `r opt("2 horizons, same switchers", "mathematics", par = "Placebo_1")` on the common set of switchers, and `r hz(2, "mathematics", rg = "full-day")` against `r hz(2, "mathematics", par = "Placebo_1", rg = "full-day")` in the full-day arm. The comparison is like for like by construction: this estimator's placebos mirror its post-treatment estimators, contrasting the same switchers against the same comparison group before adoption [@dechaisemartindyn2026]. This is the sensitivity analysis available for the primary estimand, and it is a diagnostic one rather than a formal bound: departures from parallel trends no larger than those already visible before treatment would suffice to account for the positive estimates. It is not a robust confidence set, and placebos estimate pre-treatment differences rather than post-treatment bias, so it is not a claim that each positive estimate *is* biased.

Every positive estimate reaching conventional significance here is in mathematics; none is in language, and they do not fail in the same way, which is why they are separated rather than counted. The pooled estimate fails twice: its significance exists only in the two-horizon window and re-weighting to the pupil removes it (@sec-results-headline), and its own second placebo is significant and larger than the effect it precedes. The full-day arm survives both perturbations and fails on the diagnostic alone (@sec-results-diagnosis). The doubly-robust estimate reaches conventional significance only without covariates, at `r mn("CS (absorbing)", "mathematics", cov = "none")` (s.e. `r mn("CS (absorbing)", "mathematics", "se", cov = "none")`): conditioning on the baseline covariates takes it to `r mn("CS (absorbing)", "mathematics", cov = "composition")`, re-weighting to the pupil to `r mn("CS (grade-6-weighted)", "mathematics", cov = "composition")`, and clustering that specification at the province raises its standard error from `r cl("CS (robustness)", "mathematics", "school")` to `r cl("CS (robustness)", "mathematics", "province")`.

What the data support is therefore a conclusion rather than a coefficient: there is no robustly identified evidence that the expansion of the school day raised grade-6 achievement in mathematics or language. That is not the claim that the effect is zero. Across estimator families on the common sample the union of the 95% intervals runs from `r uni("lo")` to `r uni("hi")` standard deviations, which contains effects that would matter for policy in either direction, and the design cannot exclude them. Conventional significance thresholds do no adjudicating work in that conclusion, and could not: with `r n_prov` unequal jurisdictions and an effective number near `r eff_sw`, analytic and resampled province-level uncertainty differ materially for every estimator admitting both, so which side of a threshold an estimate falls on is a property of the procedure as much as of the data. One design condition for reading a repeated cross-section this way is met: grade progression, measured annually in the census with twelve pre-treatment periods, does not move under treatment (Appendix C), so the pool of pupils sitting the assessment is not being reconfigured.

## Heterogeneity by socioeconomic disadvantage {#sec-results-hetero}

The dimensions were fixed before results were examined, with one confirmatory hypothesis — that effects are larger in more disadvantaged schools — and the remainder descriptive. Because the average effect is not robustly identified, subgroup estimates inherit that problem and are compounded by it, since every split reduces the number of identifying treatment changes; they are reported as exploratory.

The direction predicted does appear, in two measures built from different sources (@fig-hetero). On the assessment's own socioeconomic index the mathematics gradient is monotone, from `r het("SES tercile", 1, "mathematics")` in the lowest tercile to `r het("SES tercile", 3, "mathematics")` in the highest, and it survives the diagnostic exclusion of the 2023 cohort. On the official vulnerability quartile the pattern is not a gradient but a detached first quartile: mathematics is `r het("context quartile", 1, "mathematics")` in the most disadvantaged quartile against `r het("context quartile", 2, "mathematics")`, `r het("context quartile", 3, "mathematics")` and `r het("context quartile", 4, "mathematics")` in the other three. That pattern is not the 2023 artefact: excluding the cohort widens the gap between the extreme quartiles from `r itx("mathematics", "Q1 vs Q4", col = "diff")` to `r itx("mathematics", "Q1 vs Q4", "excl. 2023 cohort", col = "diff")` rather than closing it. Neither contrast is significant at conventional levels in either subject, on either sample (*p* = `r itx("mathematics", "Q1 vs Q4")` and `r itx("mathematics", "Q1 vs Q4", "excl. 2023 cohort")` in mathematics).

Estimates by region are reported with their identifying support rather than interpreted: the Northeast, which carries the mathematics pre-treatment concern of @sec-results-diagnosis, rests on `r hetn("region", "NEA", "mathematics")` switching schools in the first horizon. What the analysis shows is a compensatory *pattern in the point estimates*, consistent across two measures and marginal in every test of it, and not a compensatory effect.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hetero
#| fig-cap: "Estimated effects by subgroup, split-sample."
exhibit_fig("10_heterogeneity.png")
```

```{=latex}
\fignote{Bars are 95\% confidence intervals. Each panel is one pre-specified dimension; the split is made on the full estimation sample and each subgroup is estimated separately with the primary estimator, so the intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Because the average effect is not robustly identified, these are point estimates and not causal claims; the switcher counts supporting each cell are in the heterogeneity grid of Appendix C.}
```

# Robustness and sensitivity {#sec-robustness}

## Robustness: alternative implementations {#sec-rob-implement}

The tables carry the grid; the prose explains only the checks that change how the result is read. Nothing in how the treatment is defined does: `r n_treatdef` constructions of the binary indicator hold the same sign and order of magnitude in both subjects, with the primary estimate at the bottom of the range the cut-offs span and each paired with its own placebo (@tbl-rob-treatdef). The cut-off does little work because the share is close to dichotomous at 0 and 1, so a line at 50% sits in a sparse region.

The outcome scale, the never-treated comparison group and the socioeconomic covariate leave the estimates where they are (@tbl-rob-specs). The comparison group leaves the pre-treatment difference where it is as well: restricting the controls to schools that never switch reproduces the primary specification's second placebo almost exactly, `r plc("CDH (never-switchers)", "combined", "mathematics", k = 2)` against `r plc("CDH (headline)", "combined", "mathematics", k = 2)` in mathematics, so it is not an independently clean specification but the same one seen against a different control pool. One choice does not leave them there, and it moves the two subjects in opposite directions: restricting to schools where grade-6 exposure is arithmetically certain takes language from `r ga("full", "Language")` to `r ga("grade-6-certain", "Language")` and mathematics from `r ga("full", "Mathematics")` to `r ga("grade-6-certain", "Mathematics")`.

Wave composition is the one that does change the reading, and it is diagnostic rather than robustness (@tbl-rob-covid): dropping a wave re-dates adoption and, because event time is indexed in waves, re-spaces it. Removing the 2022 sample wave turns the primary estimator negative in both subjects, to `r cvr("drop 2022 (sample wave)", "cdh_lang")` and `r cvr("drop 2022 (sample wave)", "cdh_math")`; removing the pandemic-disrupted waves takes mathematics to `r cvr("drop 2021+2022 (COVID period)", "cdh_math")`. A re-spaced event time estimates a different parameter, so neither overturns the estimates — but both establish that the positive sign rests on a six-wave structure containing a sample wave. Deleting waves does not address the pandemic either: it enlarges the very cohort whose untreated comparison spans the recovery, which is why no explicit pandemic control is used.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rob-treatdef
#| tbl-cap: "Treatment definition."
# Each row pairs the effect with BOTH placebos of the SAME specification, because
# the cut-off moves a school's adoption date and therefore moves all three. The
# second placebo is the one that matters: for the headline it is the second, not
# the first, that rejects, so a grid showing only the first would clear every
# cut-off on half its pre-treatment evidence -- which is what this table did until
# 04 was corrected to request every placebo the window admits.
if (!is.null(.th)) {
  ord <- c("any (>0)", "0.40", "0.50 (headline)", "0.60", "0.75 (data valley)")
  labs <- c("Any expanded share ($>$ 0)", "Share $\\geq$ 40\\%",
            "Share $\\geq$ 50\\% (headline)", "Share $\\geq$ 60\\%",
            "Share $\\geq$ 75\\%")
  g <- function(tr, s) .th[threshold == tr & subject == s]
  cell <- function(s, e, v) as.vector(rbind(
    vapply(ord, function(tr) sprintf("%.3f", g(tr, s)[[e]]), character(1)),
    vapply(ord, function(tr) sprintf("(%.3f)", g(tr, s)[[v]]), character(1))))
  tab <- data.table(
    Definition = as.vector(rbind(labs, "")),
    Switchers  = as.vector(rbind(vapply(ord, function(tr)
                   fmtn(g(tr, "mathematics")$switchers1), character(1)), "")),
    a = cell("language",    "att",      "se"),
    b = cell("language",    "placebo1", "placebo1_se"),
    c = cell("language",    "placebo2", "placebo2_se"),
    d = cell("mathematics", "att",      "se"),
    e = cell("mathematics", "placebo1", "placebo1_se"),
    f = cell("mathematics", "placebo2", "placebo2_se"))
  kbl(tab, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", escape = FALSE,
      align = c("l", "r", rep("r", 6)),
      col.names = c("Treatment definition", "Switchers",
                    "(1)", "(2)", "(3)", "(4)", "(5)", "(6)")) |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 9) |>
    add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Effect" = 1, "Placebo 1" = 1, "Placebo 2" = 1,
                       "Effect" = 1, "Placebo 1" = 1, "Placebo 2" = 1)) |>
    add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Language" = 3, "Mathematics" = 3)) |>
    tbl_note(
      "The primary estimator re-run under alternative cut-offs, each paired with both pre-treatment placebos of the same specification. Standard errors in parentheses. Outcome in standard-deviation units of the ",
      "2016 anchored scale. Estimator: de Chaisemartin--D'Haultf\\\\oe uille ",
      "\\\\texttt{did\\\\_multiplegt\\\\_dyn} throughout, deliberately: moving the cut-off ",
      "moves a school's adoption date, which a design without event time cannot ",
      "detect. Comparison group not-yet-treated, aggregating the first two ",
      "post-treatment horizons, variance analytical at the school. The placebos are ",
      "the estimator's own first and second pre-treatment coefficients for the same ",
      "specification; the design admits two, and reading only the first would clear ",
      "each cut-off on half its pre-treatment evidence. In mathematics the second ",
      "exceeds the effect it precedes at every cut-off. ",
      "The switcher count is the mathematics sample at the first horizon; the ",
      "language count differs by at most a dozen schools. Every row is a ",
      "contemporaneous binary indicator on the expanded share, built the same ",
      "way as the headline, so the grid varies coverage alone.")
} else exhibit_tbl("04_threshold_sensitivity_cdh.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rob-specs
#| tbl-cap: "Full specification grid: estimators, regimes, covariate sets and the enrolment-weighted estimand."
# Panelled by estimator family rather than listed flat, because the families do
# not estimate a common parameter on an identical population and a flat list
# invites reading down the column as if they did.
if (!is.null(.m)) {
  spec <- list(
    A = list(c("CDH (headline)", "combined", "none (absorbed)", "Headline: main binary, not-yet-treated"),
             c("CDH (headline)", "full-day", "none (absorbed)", "Full-day only"),
             c("CDH (never-switchers)", "combined", "none (absorbed)", "Never-treated comparison group"),
             c("CDH (grade-6-weighted)", "combined", "none (absorbed)", "Weighted by grade-6 enrolment (pupil-average estimand)")),
    B = list(c("CS (absorbing)", "combined", "none", "No covariates"),
             c("CS (absorbing)", "combined", "structural", "Structural covariates"),
             c("CS (absorbing)", "combined", "none (comp-sample)", "No covariates, common sample"),
             c("CS (absorbing)", "combined", "composition", "Composition covariates"),
             c("CS (grade-6-weighted)", "combined", "composition", "Weighted by grade-6 enrolment (pupil-average estimand)")),
    C = list(c("TWFE (benchmark)", "combined", "none (absorbed)", "Two-way fixed effects")))
  row1 <- function(r) {
    g <- function(s) .m[estimator == r[1] & regime == r[2] & subject == s &
                        covariates == r[3]]
    num <- function(v) if (length(v) == 0 || is.na(v)) NA_real_ else v
    list(lab = r[4], n = num(g("mathematics")$n_schools),
         el = num(g("language")$att),    sl = num(g("language")$se),
         em = num(g("mathematics")$att), sm = num(g("mathematics")$se))
  }
  blk <- function(rs) {
    z <- lapply(rs, row1)
    data.table(
      Specification = as.vector(rbind(vapply(z, `[[`, character(1), "lab"), "")),
      Schools = as.vector(rbind(
        vapply(z, function(x) if (is.na(x$n)) "" else fmtn(round(x$n)), character(1)),
        rep("", length(z)))),
      Language = as.vector(rbind(
        vapply(z, function(x) if (is.na(x$el)) "--" else sprintf("%.3f", x$el), character(1)),
        vapply(z, function(x) if (is.na(x$sl)) "" else sprintf("(%.3f)", x$sl), character(1)))),
      Mathematics = as.vector(rbind(
        vapply(z, function(x) if (is.na(x$em)) "--" else sprintf("%.3f", x$em), character(1)),
        vapply(z, function(x) if (is.na(x$sm)) "" else sprintf("(%.3f)", x$sm), character(1)))))
  }
  A <- blk(spec$A); B <- blk(spec$B); C <- blk(spec$C)
  tab <- rbind(A, B, C)
  kbl(tab, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
      col.names = c("Specification", "Schools", "(1)", "(2)")) |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 10) |>
    add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Language" = 1, "Mathematics" = 1)) |>
    pack_rows("Panel A. Primary estimator (CDH)", 1, nrow(A)) |>
    pack_rows("Panel B. Doubly robust (Callaway--Sant'Anna), absorbing subsample",
              nrow(A) + 1, nrow(A) + nrow(B), escape = FALSE) |>
    pack_rows("Panel C. Benchmark", nrow(A) + nrow(B) + 1, nrow(tab)) |>
    tbl_note(
      "Standard errors in parentheses, N (school-waves) beneath them. Outcome in ",
      "standard-deviation units of the ",
      "2016 anchored scale. Unless a row states otherwise: the main binary ",
      "treatment (expanded share $\\\\geq$ 50\\\\% in the year), not-yet-treated ",
      "comparison group, unweighted school means, first two post-treatment ",
      "horizons, variance analytical at the school. Panel B is ",
      "fitted on the subsample that never contracts, which the estimator's ",
      "absorbing-adoption assumption requires, so its schools are not the schools ",
      "of Panel A; the school count is blank where the estimator does not report ",
      "one. Baseline covariates appear only in Panel B because the primary ",
      "estimator differences within school, so a time-invariant covariate has ",
      "$\\\\Delta X = 0$ and drops out. Two-way fixed effects is reported as a ",
      "benchmark and is not expected to identify the estimand. Weighting re-targets ",
      "the estimand from the school to the pupil and is not a robustness check; the ",
      "primary-enrolment weights give the same answer as the grade-6 weights shown ",
      "here, and are in the committed output rather than in this table.")
} else exhibit_tbl("06_estimation_main.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rob-covid
#| tbl-cap: "Wave composition."
# The primary estimator reports no standard error in this output, so its columns
# carry the point estimate alone and the note says so rather than leaving the
# reader to infer that the parentheses were forgotten.
if (!is.null(.cvr)) {
  ord <- c("full (6 waves, headline)", "drop 2021 (COVID trough)",
           "drop 2021+2022 (COVID period)", "drop 2022 (sample wave)",
           "exclude 2023 cohort (full waves)")
  labs <- c("Full panel (six waves, headline)", "Drop 2021 (pandemic trough)",
            "Drop 2021 and 2022 (pandemic period)", "Drop 2022 (sample wave)",
            "Exclude the 2023 adoption cohort")
  g <- function(sp) .cvr[spec == sp]
  pt <- function(col) vapply(ord, function(sp) {
    v <- g(sp)[[col]]; if (length(v) == 0 || is.na(v)) "--" else sprintf("%.3f", v) },
    character(1))
  pair <- function(e, v) as.vector(rbind(pt(e), vapply(ord, function(sp) {
    x <- g(sp)[[v]]; if (length(x) == 0 || is.na(x)) "" else sprintf("(%.3f)", x) },
    character(1))))
  tab <- data.table(
    Sample = as.vector(rbind(labs, "")),
    Waves  = as.vector(rbind(vapply(ord, function(sp)
               as.character(length(strsplit(g(sp)$waves, ",")[[1]])), character(1)), "")),
    a = as.vector(rbind(pt("cdh_lang"), "")),
    b = as.vector(rbind(pt("cdh_math"), "")),
    c = pair("cs_lang", "cs_lang_se"),
    d = pair("cs_math", "cs_math_se"))
  kbl(tab, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
      col.names = c("Wave composition", "Waves", "(1)", "(2)", "(3)", "(4)")) |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position") |>
    add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Language" = 1, "Mathematics" = 1,
                       "Language" = 1, "Mathematics" = 1)) |>
    add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Primary estimator (CDH)" = 2,
                       "Doubly robust (CS)" = 2)) |>
    tbl_note(
      "The primary and doubly-robust estimators re-run dropping the pandemic-disrupted waves, dropping the 2022 sample wave, and excluding the 2023 adoption cohort. Outcome in standard-deviation units of the 2016 anchored scale. Standard ",
      "errors in parentheses for columns (3) and (4); columns (1) and (2) report ",
```

## Sensitivity to the identifying assumptions {#sec-rob-sensitivity}

Not whether the answer depends on implementation choices, but how large a violation of the identifying assumption would overturn it.

Clustering at the province returns smaller analytic standard errors for the primary estimator than clustering at the school in `r shrink_n` of the `r shrink_of` reported cells — `r cl("CDH (primary)", "mathematics", "province")` against `r cl("CDH (primary)", "mathematics", "school")` for the pooled mathematics estimate. The `r num_word(shrink_of - shrink_n)` cells that move the other way are both in mathematics: the first post-treatment horizon and the most distant placebo. That is not by itself inconsistent with cluster-robust variance estimation: the formula sums group-level contributions within a province before squaring them, so contributions that offset can lower the estimate, and no result guarantees that coarser clusters give larger errors. What the shrinkage puts in doubt is the approximation, not the level, because the effective provincial support is small. Resampling at that level returns materially larger errors — `r cb("mathematics", "ATE", "se_boot_package")` against the analytic `r cb("mathematics", "ATE", "se_province")` for the pooled mathematics estimate — and the disagreement is large enough to matter: the same point estimate carries *t* = `r cbt("mathematics", "ATE", "se_province")` analytically and *t* = `r cbt("mathematics", "ATE")` under the bootstrap. The mathematics second placebo moves the same way, from *t* = `r cbt("mathematics", "Placebo_2", "se_school")` to `r cbt("mathematics", "Placebo_2")`. Effect and placebo lose conventional significance together, which is why the diagnostic of @sec-results-verdict compares magnitudes and not significance, and why neither procedure is treated as the authoritative one.

Formal Rambachan–Roth bounds [@rambachan2023] are reported only for the doubly-robust estimator, which produces the absorbing-adoption event study the method was built for, and they pertain only to its own estimand on that subsample: they do not validate the primary estimates, whose sensitivity is the diagnostic comparison of @sec-results-verdict. Two reasons keep the method off the primary estimator, the first sufficient on its own. The joint covariance matrix of effects and placebos that the command returns is not positive semi-definite, its smallest eigenvalue being `r min_eig` — material rather than numerical, and repairing it to force the procedure through would manufacture the validity the diagnostic denies. The second is interpretive: event time is indexed by assessment waves spanning between `r wave_gap_lo` and `r wave_gap_hi` years, so a bound relating post-treatment violations to the largest pre-treatment one would carry no homogeneous temporal meaning. In `r num_word(hd_n_at(0.5))` of the four specifications the robust set already covers zero at $\bar{M}=`r hd_zero("language")`$, a post-treatment violation half the size of the largest observed pre-treatment one; uncontrolled mathematics is the exception, first covering zero at $\bar{M}=`r hd_zero("mathematics")`$. Neither is a violation the pre-treatment evidence rules out, so the localised feature of @sec-results-diagnosis surfaces as formal sensitivity rather than unexplained width. An equivalence test tells the same story from the other side: it asks whether pre-treatment effects lie inside a pre-specified bound rather than treating a non-rejection as support [@roth2022]. Under a strict 0.05-standard-deviation bound, mathematics achieves equivalence and language does not, while the package's default bounds are too wide to be informative (Appendix B).

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

Four limitations bear on what has been estimated, in order of how much they constrain it.

**The sign depends on the counterfactual trend.** Estimators that compare against not-yet-treated schools give small positives; estimators that impose one common trend give negatives (@sec-rob-sensitivity). The disagreement survives the two explanations tested for it (@sec-results-diagnosis), and traces mostly to one adoption cohort. But that is an attribution, not a resolution: the cohort is also the largest single source of identifying variation, so it cannot be removed without changing the estimand, and every result that excludes it is a probe rather than a preferred estimate.

**The estimand is local to assessed schools.** *Aprender* does not reach the smallest schools, and the same size-dependent coverage decides which schools appear in a later wave — and so support a longer horizon at all (@sec-data-sources). The weighted estimates show only that the per-school effect does not carry over proportionally to the per-pupil one; they do not show that effects are larger in small schools, which would require holding rurality, composition, province and cohort fixed.

**Measurement error, and not classical.** Some `r fhm("of which left in the comparison group")` five-hour schools sit in the comparison group, and the misclassification is clustered by jurisdiction and correlated with cohort. The resulting bias is of unknown sign and magnitude: contamination of the comparison group would compress the contrast only under monotone positive effects, and neither holds here — so these estimates are not a lower bound.

**A school-level intention to treat.** The parameter compares schools by the regime they operate, not by the hours any grade-6 cohort received, and treatment is recorded over the whole primary cycle rather than grade 6 alone (@sec-strategy-estimand). Arithmetic forces grade-6 exposure in most treated school-years, and restricting to the schools where it is certain moves the two subjects in opposite directions (@sec-rob-implement) — so misalignment does not generate the results. But the estimates are not invariant to it: peer effects, resource reallocation and compositional change can move the school- and pupil-level parameters apart in either direction.

# Conclusion {#sec-discussion}

This dissertation asked whether the expansion of extended- and full-day schooling raised grade-6 achievement in Argentine primary education, and for whom. Three answers follow. First, the administrative statistics used to monitor expansion do not cleanly measure genuine extension of the school day: the RA records many five-hour schools under the same category as genuine six-hour extension, does so unevenly across jurisdictions, and the federal programme sharply increased the number of schools at precisely that measurement margin. Second, the data do not provide robustly identified evidence that the expansion raised achievement in either subject. The pooled event-time estimate combines schools observed at materially different calendar distances from their first switch, and the corresponding pooled placebo can conceal offsetting pre-treatment differences across those timing classes. More generally, estimators that impose different counterfactual trends do not agree, and the diagnostics explain enough of that disagreement to prevent any single positive estimate from carrying the causal conclusion. Third, effects tend to be larger in more disadvantaged schools across two independently constructed measures, but the evidence is too imprecise for more than an exploratory pattern in the point estimates. The central methodological lesson is therefore not that one modern estimator dominates another, but that the diagnostics determine how much causal weight any of them can bear.

A null is not an absence of information here, and the theory says why: if instructional time is an input with diminishing returns, an additional hour buys most where the day is shortest (@sec-lit-time), and Argentina's *jornada simple* is a four-hour shift day, so the prior was favourable. It is expensive information — abandoning a shift system raises the cost of primary provision by between a quarter and three-fifths [@orkin2013], and regional reviews already judged extended-day reform less cost-effective than the alternatives [@holland2015; @contreras2023] — so a null matters precisely because the policy continues to absorb a substantial budget [@arzola2011]. What it does not settle is whether the policy is worth its cost: the same literature documents more consistent effects on dropout, on socio-emotional outcomes and on maternal labour supply [@berthelon2011; @contreras2023], none of which this design measures, so a null on test scores removes the justification most often invoked for the longer day and not the others. Those outcomes are where the case for the policy may well rest, and where the next study should look.

Three fronts follow, and on each the implication and the research it calls for are one point rather than two. On measurement, the coverage statistics reported against a twenty-year legal commitment do not measure the thing the commitment is about, and the fix is administrative rather than methodological: a census item recording daily hours, or participation in the specific programme, would supply directly what this dissertation had to reconstruct from a director questionnaire. On content, the additional hours were mandated for reading, writing and mathematical literacy [@cfe426_2022; @cfe470_2024] and no gain in those domains is detected, which points the binding question at what happens inside the added time rather than at how much time is added — the conditionality the cross-national evidence has repeatedly found [@lavy2015; @rivkin2015; @ganimian2016] — and separating a lengthened day from a changed one would require classroom-level data the administrative sources do not carry. On implementation, adoption is not permanent, so a policy evaluated as though adoption were an absorbing transition is being evaluated for something that did not happen: a constraint on the estimand rather than a main finding, but the feature a ministry can act on most directly.

What this dissertation establishes about achievement is bounded and worth stating exactly. The data do not support the claim that expanding the school day raised grade-6 performance in mathematics or language. They also do not support the claim that the effect is zero: the intervals across estimators remain wide enough to contain effects that would matter for policy in either direction. Given that the policy has been national law for two decades and that the statistics used to report progress towards it measure something else, both halves of that sentence are findings.

Two implementation details qualify what the doubly-robust specification means. Both concern the subsample it is fitted on rather than the identification of the primary estimand.

The first is which schools it drops. Callaway--Sant'Anna requires absorbing treatment, so it is fitted on schools that never contract — but "never contracts" is evaluated on the six assessment waves rather than on the annual census, so a school that adopts, contracts and re-adopts between two waves is retained. The two readings are far apart: `r rv("6 outcome waves only (estimation sample)")`% of ever-treated schools revert when reversal is measured across waves, against `r rv("RA annual history (all schools)")`% on the annual record (@tbl-reversion), and the annual figure is the correct one because reversal is a property of that record. The subsample is therefore absorbing *as observed at the assessment waves* rather than absorbing in fact, so the claim that the estimator's identifying assumption holds by construction is exact only for the specifications built on the annual rule.

The second is how its adoption cohorts are dated: by the first wave at which a school is observed treated, not by the calendar year of adoption. Because the 2022 wave is a sample rather than a census, only schools drawn into it can belong to that cohort, which holds `r csz(2022)` schools against `r csz(2023)` in the cohort that follows it. Membership there is decided by the assessment's sampling design rather than by when a school adopted, and the cell is smaller still in the doubly-robust subsample — small enough to be what makes that estimator fail at the 75% cut-off, which is why the treatment-definition grid is estimated with the primary estimator instead (@tbl-rob-treatdef).

The exhibits below support @sec-results-rollout: separating genuine six-hour extension from the five-hour day leaves the mathematics pre-trend in place (@fig-app-genuine), against the counts of each schedule among the schools the census records as extended in 2023 (@tbl-contamination). @fig-intensity shows what the binary indicator is tracking on the annual record.

## B. Estimator disagreement and identification {.unnumbered}

These exhibits support @sec-results-diagnosis. The dynamic profile is erratic rather than accumulating (@fig-app-fectdyn); matched event time shows the two estimator families diverging on the same sample (@tbl-app-matched, @tbl-lfl), on estimates whose full-sample counterparts are in @tbl-fect; the carryover and lead-by-lead forensics reject the two candidate explanations (@tbl-app-carryover, @tbl-app-leads, @tbl-excl2023); and the identifying-variation check shows that the convergence observed after excluding the 2023 cohort is not merely a loss of identifying variation (@tbl-app-idvar). @tbl-app-cdhboot and @tbl-app-resampling carry the province-level inference of @sec-rob-sensitivity.

Equivalence testing under the package's default bounds is uninformative: the thresholds `r ft("language equivalence (default bound)", "tost_threshold")` and `r ft("maths equivalence (default bound)", "tost_threshold")` are several times the effects being tested. Under a strict bound of 0.05 standard deviations both subjects achieve equivalence, at *p* = `r ft("language equivalence (bound 0.05)", "tost_equiv_p")` in language and *p* = `r ft("maths equivalence (bound 0.05)", "tost_equiv_p")` in mathematics: every pre-treatment period lies inside the bound, even though the joint test rejects zero.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-app-resampling
#| tbl-cap: "Province-level resampling inference for the regression-based estimators."
.rsx <- read_out("06f_resampling.csv")
if (!is.null(.rsx)) {
  gv <- function(est, subj, lv, inf, col) {
    v <- .rsx[estimator %like% est & subject == subj & cluster_level == lv &
              inference %like% inf][[col]]
    if (length(v) == 0) NA_real_ else v[1]
  }
  fm <- function(x, d = 3) if (is.na(x)) "---" else sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x)
  spec <- list(list("TWFE", "wild", "wild cluster"), list("FEct", "nonparametric", "pairs cluster"))
  tab <- rbindlist(lapply(spec, function(s) rbindlist(lapply(c("language", "mathematics"), function(sb) {
    # TWFE's school and province columns are the analytic cluster-robust errors;
    # FEct has no analytic variance, so both of its columns are bootstrap errors.
    ia <- if (s[[1]] == "TWFE") "analytic" else "nonparametric"
    lo <- gv(s[[1]], sb, "province", s[[2]], "ci_lo"); hi <- gv(s[[1]], sb, "province", s[[2]], "ci_hi")
    data.table(Estimator = s[[1]], Subject = sb,
               Estimate      = fm(gv(s[[1]], sb, "school", ia, "att")),
               `s.e. school` = fm(gv(s[[1]], sb, "school", ia, "se")),
               `s.e. prov.`  = fm(gv(s[[1]], sb, "province", ia, "se")),
               `p analytic`  = if (s[[1]] == "TWFE")
                                 fm(gv(s[[1]], sb, "province", "analytic", "p")) else "---",
               `p resampled` = fm(gv(s[[1]], sb, "province", s[[2]], "p")),
               `95\\% CI`    = if (is.na(lo)) "---" else sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", lo, hi),
               Scheme        = s[[3]])
  }))))
  kbl(tab, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", escape = FALSE,
      align = c("l", "l", rep("r", 5), "c", "l")) |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position", "scale_down")) |>
    tbl_note(paste0(
      "The resampling scheme is not the same for the two, and the difference is a property of the estimand rather than a choice. Estimation sample, both estimators on the same panel, treatment as defined in ",
      "\\S4.2. TWFE is a static two-way fixed-effects coefficient, so its school and ",
      "province columns are analytic cluster-robust errors and its resampled column is ",
      "the restricted wild cluster bootstrap with Rademacher weights, 999 replications, ",
      "with the interval obtained by test inversion. FEct has no analytic variance: both ",
      "of its standard errors are nonparametric cluster bootstraps, at the school and at ",
      "the province, 1,000 replications. The wild scheme is defined on regression ",
      "residuals and is the better behaved of the two with few clusters, so only the ",
      "linear model can receive it. The resampled p-values are therefore NOT comparable ",
      "across the two estimators as measures of evidential strength."))
} else kbl(data.frame(Status = "exhibit pending: 06f_resampling.csv"),
           booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "")
```

## C. Secondary outcomes and heterogeneity {.unnumbered}

**Grade-progression trajectories: a composition check.** The census supplies a secondary outcome measured annually rather than in waves, with twelve pre-treatment periods instead of two. Neither component moves: non-promotion is `r np_att` percentage points (95% CI `r np_lo` to `r np_hi`) against an untreated mean of `r np_base`, and dropout is indistinguishable from zero in every specification (@tbl-app-traj, @fig-traj). This is a design check more than a result. A repeated cross-section is threatened by the possibility that the measured average moved because a different kind of pupil sat the assessment, and treatment that leaves repetition and dropout unchanged does not reconfigure the pool being tested — evidence of compositional non-response, not a test of parallel trends in test scores.

The same secondary outcome invites comparison with the closest Argentine antecedent, but the two are less comparable than they first appear. Nistal (2022) reports a 23% reduction in grade retention over 2011--2019, on a broader object than this design targets: retention pooled across all primary grades, under a treatment that counts any extended-regime enrolment, and excluding full-day schools. What this dissertation observes is narrower — grade-6 non-promotion at the primary threshold — and because retention concentrates in the early grades, a grade-6 null neither reproduces nor contradicts a primary-wide reduction. Applied to the untreated mean here their relative effect would be about `r np_en` percentage points, below the lower bound of the interval above; but the difference in grade coverage, treatment definition and sample makes this a point of context, not a replication test.

The exhibits below carry the full grade-progression results across specifications, and the complete heterogeneity grid supporting @sec-results-hetero (@tbl-app-hetero), with the 2023-cohort exclusion repeated within each subgroup and the pre-specified interaction test in @tbl-app-interaction.
